title: A Managed Database-as-a-Service Platform for Scientific Computing
authors: Jingyan Jiang; Huihuo Zheng; Venkatram Vishwanath
source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Scientific computing at HPC facilities increasingly relies on database infrastructure across a growing range of workloads: vector search and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG), structured analytics, and AI-driven knowledge discovery over community corpora spanning documentation, experimental datasets, simulation outputs, and literature collections. These corpora are inherently shared facility resources, serving researchers, facility support staff, and AI agents across projects and institutions. Yet the supporting infrastructure remains built per project: each team provisions, configures, and operates its own database instance, with no facility-level registry, no shared identity layer, and no uniform interface for discovering or accessing the databases hosted across the facility. Commercial cloud platforms have addressed analogous needs through managed Database-as-a-Service offerings (e.g., Amazon RDS, Snowflake, Pinecone). However, these solutions do not transfer cleanly to scientific computing: they rely on proprietary identity systems, cannot directly access facility filesystems, and incur substantial data egress costs. We are building the missing piece: a managed database platform that lives inside the HPC facility, developed and evaluated on ALCF Polaris. One federated sign-in (Globus) brings a researcher — or an AI agent acting on their behalf — to every database the facility hosts, through a web UI, a scriptable API, or the Model Context Protocol. Governance, catalog, and access control are handled once by the platform and inherited by every project by default. The central design choice is scaling, native to HPC. Each workload is decomposed into its resource-consuming stages, and each stage can be scaled independently across nodes. As one representative example, a vector-search workload scales GPU-based embedding generation and search-index serving independently across nodes, reaching 5,197 queries/sec on 8 nodes (4.3× single-node) on ALCF Polaris and still climbing at maximum tested concurrency. Governance adds modest overhead at single-user load and becomes negligible under concurrency. In an end-to-end RAG pipeline built on this workload, retrieval contributes under 2% of total latency — the bottleneck has moved entirely to LLM generation. The same decomposition pattern is designed to extend to other workload types as additional engine adapters are integrated. The talk presents what changes when scientific data services are native to the facility: who can use them, what AI agents become capable of, and how a single platform can replace per-project infrastructure across an entire lab. We will share the design tradeoffs, what the scaling numbers mean for facility capacity planning, and the next stage of the design — co-locating the database service with model-inference services and scaling both on demand against shared facility resources, planned for the coming year. We invite peer facilities to adopt the platform and collaborate with us on a unified, cross-facility scientific data service.

title: Presentation-Invariant Supplier Selection Benchmark: Open-Weight LLM Decision Reliability Under Multi-Objective Conflict
authors: Ryan SangBaek Kim
source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Reproducibility package for the study “Presentation-Invariant Supplier Selection? Stress-Testing Open-Weight LLM Decision Reliability Under Multi-Objective Conflict,” accepted for presentation at ICLIE 2026. The benchmark evaluates whether open-weight large language models preserve supplier-selection decisions when all decision-relevant information is held constant and only supplier-row order changes. The release contains six independently generated base scenarios, four controlled multi-objective conflict levels, three balanced row-order presentations, and evaluations of three open-weight LLMs, yielding 216 main model calls. The package includes frozen benchmark scenarios, exact prompts, sanitized raw model outputs, scoring and analysis code, identical-input robustness data, design-freeze records, and peer-review revision analyses. The revision-stage statistical analysis treats the six base scenarios as the independent experimental units and reports scenario-cluster uncertainty estimates. No main-study observations or raw outputs were altered during revision. Data and documentation are released under CC BY 4.0; code is released under the MIT License.

title: PREreview of "Argo-Bench: Evaluating Data Agents on Enterprise-Scale Workflows"
authors: Karmendra Pandey
source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/23129439. ## Summary This paper argues that current data-agent benchmarks measure the wrong thing: text-to-SQL accuracy over small public schemas, with answer keys that a recent audit found wrong more often than right. In response, the authors build Argo-Bench — a simulated 2024 New York City food-delivery platform (81M orders, 3.4M customers) projected into a 235-table, 7.49-billion-row Oracle E-Business Suite warehouse — and define 210 tasks across fraud detection, forecasting, financial planning, dashboards, and compliance. The decisive design choice is consequence-based grading: the simulator's latent state is withheld from the agent, and filings (ban lists, forecasts, budget allocations, dashboard sources) are scored by their simulated consequences — fraud losses prevented net of wrongly-banned revenue, weighted interval scores against held-out months, share of attainable savings realized — rather than by matching a gold answer. The best of 14 frontier and open models (Claude Opus 5.5) solves 34.8% of tasks at ≥95 and averages 59.5/100. The paper's most valuable contribution may be its failure taxonomy: failing runs use sound methods but read the wrong record, optimize the wrong objective, or measure the wrong quantity. ## Strengths 1. **Consequence-based grading is the right direction, executed seriously.** Scoring a ban list by fraud losses prevented (including undetected fraud) net of destroyed customer margin — with explicit review costs and appeals modeling via Elkan-style example-dependent costs — is a genuine advance over answer-key matching. It aligns the benchmark's objective with the business objective, which is precisely what enterprise buyers care about. 2. **Unusual methodological honesty.** The limitations section and the Appendix J task audit openly document where the benchmark is weak: re-keyed tasks, realigned prompts, a fraud family the authors admit "tests less than it was designed to," and the explicit statement that the benchmark "compares data agents and does not estimate their performance on a real company's warehouse." This level of self-audit is rare and commendable. 3. **The failure taxonomy is practitioner gold.** The "wrong record / wrong objective / wrong quantity" analysis (Section 3.2) — e.g., 24 runs taking membership status from contract dates while the correct definition required replaying billing history through a seven-day grace rule — diagnoses exactly how production data agents fail: on semantics and business definitions, not on SQL syntax. Any enterprise data leader should read this section. 4. **Serious simulation craft.** 34 donor datasets with explicit identity/shape/anchor roles, calibration to NYC DCWP quarterly anchors (per-delivery economics within 5% in 13 of 16 comparisons), a real extrinsic shock (the April 2024 minimum-pay increase) enabling genuine forecasting tasks, schema verified against Oracle EBS 12.2 Vision with three ERP consultants, and an explicit no-LLM-generated-records policy. The two-seed design (public warehouse, private leaderboard world) is the right defense against memorization. 5. **Cost accounting in Appendix K is exemplary.** Reporting that warehouse spend ($6,160) was the same order as model API spend ($14,502) — and that for cheap models the warehouse was 70–92% of total cost — is the kind of honest economics the field needs. ## Major concerns **1. The simulator's response model is the new gold answer.** The paper's central claim is that consequence grading escapes the tyranny of annotator answer keys. But for the five quest-cut tasks, the reference loss LrefL_{ref} is "the optimal plan itself" *under the simulator's response model* — a score of 100 means the agent recovered the optimum of the authors' own causal assumptions. An agent that reverse-engineers the response model scores perfectly, which rewards simulator-fitting rather than real-world judgment. The authors are aware of the general problem (they cite Leis et al. on shared simplifying assumptions), but the paper never tests robustness: how much do rankings change if the response model's parameters are perturbed? Without that, "consequences" inherits the exact fragility the paper attributes to gold answers, one level removed. **2. Inconsistent reference standards across task families.** For the four courier-hour allocation tasks, LrefL_{ref} is "the best plan the authors reached from the warehouse alone" — explicitly *not* the true optimum, which "would require information that the agent cannot obtain" — while the quest tasks use the true simulator optimum. So a score of 100 means different things in different task families: best-human-effort in one, simulator-optimum in the other. This inconsistency makes cross-family score comparisons (and the headline mean of 59.5) hard to interpret. The paper should either harmonize the standard or report families separately as primary results. **3. Seven forecast references were set with the outcome in view.** Table 7 discloses that for 7 of the 22 fixed forecast references, "the point was set with the realized value in view." These references set the *scale* on which every forecast in those series is graded. Even with honest intent, choosing scale parameters with knowledge of the outcome can compress or stretch the grading range in ways that favor particular error profiles. The authors report results without these tasks in Appendix I, which is good — but tasks whose grading scale was outcome-informed should be excluded from the headline numbers, not merely analyzed separately. **4. The headline numbers are irreproducible by design.** The simulator and graders are withheld "to prevent direct answer memorization," and all paper experiments ran on a private-seed world. Outsiders can reproduce the *procedure* on a sibling world but never the *numbers* — including the headline 34.8% / 59.5. Combined with one run per task per setting (confidence intervals "reflect the choice of tasks rather than run-to-run variation"), this means the paper's central quantitative claims rest on an experiment no independent party can repeat. The two-seed design is defensible against memorization, but the paper should acknowledge the cost: this is a benchmark whose leaderboard cannot be audited, only trusted. **5. Simulation fidelity rests on transferred assumptions the paper under-examines.** Fraud separability is calibrated from IEEE-CIS — a credit-card fraud dataset — and honest-user device/address/card sharing rates from RBA login data; both are transferred across domains to delivery-platform fraud. The membership program "rests on weakly grounded assumptions" (authors' own words). Calibration to aggregate anchors "does not guarantee realistic tails" (citing Chen et al. 2019) — and tails are precisely where fraud detection lives. None of this invalidates the benchmark for *comparing* agents, but the paper's framing sometimes implies more: the fraud tasks' precision/recall tradeoffs are only as meaningful as the transferred separability assumptions, and those deserve a sensitivity analysis, not just a limitations paragraph. **6. The warehouse is deliberately unlike real warehouses in the way that matters most.** The three ERP consultants named the absence of data drift and inconsistencies — deprecated tables overlapping active ones, figures failing to reconcile — "the most significant difference from their customers' systems," and the authors kept it clean to keep ground truth unambiguous. That is a reasonable design choice, but it means the benchmark tests greenfield warehouse *navigation* while real enterprise data work is dominated by *archaeology*: reconciling conflicting sources, decoding undocumented conventions, working around migrations. The paper should be explicit that this entire skill category is out of scope, since it is arguably the larger half of production data work. **7. The main-table cost column is misleading without the warehouse.** Table 2 reports per-task API spend ($0.06–$4.89), but Appendix K shows warehouse spend flips the economics: GPT-6 Luna's true per-task cost is $0.70, not $0.06; DeepSeek, GLM Flash, and Muse Spark 1.3 spend more on BigQuery in absolute terms than Opus does ($0.94–$1.63 vs $0.82); Muse Spark 1.3 burns $11.77 of warehouse per solved task against $2.20–$2.37 for the leaders, with 57% of its warehouse dollars spent on tasks scoring below 5. A benchmark about enterprise economics should put total cost — not API cost — in the main results table. ## Minor concerns - **34 "presence" tasks are graded on filing existence.** A note explaining the agent's work is valuable, but scoring 16% of the benchmark on whether *any* filing was made is a weak grading mode that inflates scores for verbosity-adjacent behavior. - **The Appendix J audit reveals post-hoc key surgery.** Two task families required re-keying (138 of 249 originally-keyed couriers were already deactivated; a misweighted composite score) *after* runs were examined, with everything regraded and rerun. The transparency is admirable, but it raises the question the paper doesn't answer: how many keys would a truly independent auditor find, and should the audit be a living document rather than a one-time appendix? - **The injected-refund shortcut (Appendix J) weakens a headline fraud family.** All 664 anomalous refunds fall within the 98 simulator-injected storefronts, so "one pass over the refunds therefore finds every candidate" — the family tests ring-vs-control discrimination, not discovery. The authors keep it "as run" because fixing it "changes the world," but a benchmark paper should quantify how much easier the task became rather than leaving it to the appendix. - **Vendor authorship deserves a sentence.** All five authors are at TextQL, which sells data-agent products. abstract: This Zenodo record is a permanently preserved version of a PREreview. You can view the complete PREreview at https://prereview.org/reviews/23129439. ## Summary This paper argues that current data-agent benchmarks measure the wrong thing: text-to-SQL accuracy over small public schemas, with answer keys that a recent audit found wrong more often than right. In response, the authors build Argo-Bench — a simulated 2024 New York City food-delivery platform (81M orders, 3.4M customers) projected into a 235-table, 7.49-billion-row Oracle E-Business Suite warehouse — and define 210 tasks across fraud detection, forecasting, financial planning, dashboards, and compliance. The decisive design choice is consequence-based grading: the simulator's latent state is withheld from the agent, and filings (ban lists, forecasts, budget allocations, dashboard sources) are scored by their simulated consequences — fraud losses prevented net of wrongly-banned revenue, weighted interval scores against held-out months, share of attainable savings realized — rather than by matching a gold answer. The best of 14 frontier and open models (Claude Opus 5.5) solves 34.8% of tasks at ≥95 and averages 59.5/100. The paper's most valuable contribution may be its failure taxonomy: failing runs use sound methods but read the wrong record, optimize the wrong objective, or measure the wrong quantity. ## Strengths 1. **Consequence-based grading is the right direction, executed seriously.** Scoring a ban list by fraud losses prevented (including undetected fraud) net of destroyed customer margin — with explicit review costs and appeals modeling via Elkan-style example-dependent costs — is a genuine advance over answer-key matching. It aligns the benchmark's objective with the business objective, which is precisely what enterprise buyers care about. 2. **Unusual methodological honesty.** The limitations section and the Appendix J task audit openly document where the benchmark is weak: re-keyed tasks, realigned prompts, a fraud family the authors admit "tests less than it was designed to," and the explicit statement that the benchmark "compares data agents and does not estimate their performance on a real company's warehouse." This level of self-audit is rare and commendable. 3. **The failure taxonomy is practitioner gold.** The "wrong record / wrong objective / wrong quantity" analysis (Section 3.2) — e.g., 24 runs taking membership status from contract dates while the correct definition required replaying billing history through a seven-day grace rule — diagnoses exactly how production data agents fail: on semantics and business definitions, not on SQL syntax. Any enterprise data leader should read this section. 4. **Serious simulation craft.** 34 donor datasets with explicit identity/shape/anchor roles, calibration to NYC DCWP quarterly anchors (per-delivery economics within 5% in 13 of 16 comparisons), a real extrinsic shock (the April 2024 minimum-pay increase) enabling genuine forecasting tasks, schema verified against Oracle EBS 12.2 Vision with three ERP consultants, and an explicit no-LLM-generated-records policy. The two-seed design (public warehouse, private leaderboard world) is the right defense against memorization. 5. **Cost accounting in Appendix K is exemplary.** Reporting that warehouse spend ($6,160) was the same order as model API spend ($14,502) — and that for cheap models the warehouse was 70–92% of total cost — is the kind of honest economics the field needs. ## Major concerns **1. The simulator's response model is the new gold answer.** The paper's central claim is that consequence grading escapes the tyranny of annotator answer keys. But for the five quest-cut tasks, the reference loss LrefL_{ref} is "the optimal plan itself" *under the simulator's response model* — a score of 100 means the agent recovered the optimum of the authors' own causal assumptions. An agent that reverse-engineers the response model scores perfectly, which rewards simulator-fitting rather than real-world judgment. The authors are aware of the general problem (they cite Leis et al. on shared simplifying assumptions), but the paper never tests robustness: how much do rankings change if the response model's parameters are perturbed? Without that, "consequences" inherits the exact fragility the paper attributes to gold answers, one level removed. **2. Inconsistent reference standards across task families.** For the four courier-hour allocation tasks, LrefL_{ref} is "the best plan the authors reached from the warehouse alone" — explicitly *not* the true optimum, which "would require information that the agent cannot obtain" — while the quest tasks use the true simulator optimum. So a score of 100 means different things in different task families: best-human-effort in one, simulator-optimum in the other. This inconsistency makes cross-family score comparisons (and the headline mean of 59.5) hard to interpret. The paper should either harmonize the standard or report families separately as primary results. **3. Seven forecast references were set with the outcome in view.** Table 7 discloses that for 7 of the 22 fixed forecast references, "the point was set with the realized value in view." These references set the *scale* on which every forecast in those series is graded. Even with honest intent, choosing scale parameters with knowledge of the outcome can compress or stretch the grading range in ways that favor particular error profiles. The authors report results without these tasks in Appendix I, which is good — but tasks whose grading scale was outcome-informed should be excluded from the headline numbers, not merely analyzed separately. **4. The headline numbers are irreproducible by design.** The simulator and graders are withheld "to prevent direct answer memorization," and all paper experiments ran on a private-seed world. Outsiders can reproduce the *procedure* on a sibling world but never the *numbers* — including the headline 34.8% / 59.5. Combined with one run per task per setting (confidence intervals "reflect the choice of tasks rather than run-to-run variation"), this means the paper's central quantitative claims rest on an experiment no independent party can repeat. The two-seed design is defensible against memorization, but the paper should acknowledge the cost: this is a benchmark whose leaderboard cannot be audited, only trusted. **5. Simulation fidelity rests on transferred assumptions the paper under-examines.** Fraud separability is calibrated from IEEE-CIS — a credit-card fraud dataset — and honest-user device/address/card sharing rates from RBA login data; both are transferred across domains to delivery-platform fraud. The membership program "rests on weakly grounded assumptions" (authors' own words). Calibration to aggregate anchors "does not guarantee realistic tails" (citing Chen et al. 2019) — and tails are precisely where fraud detection lives. None of this invalidates the benchmark for *comparing* agents, but the paper's framing sometimes implies more: the fraud tasks' precision/recall tradeoffs are only as meaningful as the transferred separability assumptions, and those deserve a sensitivity analysis, not just a limitations paragraph. **6. The warehouse is deliberately unlike real warehouses in the way that matters most.** The three ERP consultants named the absence of data drift and inconsistencies — deprecated tables overlapping active ones, figures failing to reconcile — "the most significant difference from their customers' systems," and the authors kept it clean to keep ground truth unambiguous. That is a reasonable design choice, but it means the benchmark tests greenfield warehouse *navigation* while real enterprise data work is dominated by *archaeology*: reconciling conflicting sources, decoding undocumented conventions, working around migrations. The paper should be explicit that this entire skill category is out of scope, since it is arguably the larger half of production data work. **7. The main-table cost column is misleading without the warehouse.** Table 2 reports per-task API spend ($0.06–$4.89), but Appendix K shows warehouse spend flips the economics: GPT-6 Luna's true per-task cost is $0.70, not $0.06; DeepSeek, GLM Flash, and Muse Spark 1.3 spend more on BigQuery in absolute terms than Opus does ($0.94–$1.63 vs $0.82); Muse Spark 1.3 burns $11.77 of warehouse per solved task against $2.20–$2.37 for the leaders, with 57% of its warehouse dollars spent on tasks scoring below 5. A benchmark about enterprise economics should put total cost — not API cost — in the main results table. ## Minor concerns - **34 "presence" tasks are graded on filing existence.** A note explaining the agent's work is valuable, but scoring 16% of the benchmark on whether *any* filing was made is a weak grading mode that inflates scores for verbosity-adjacent behavior. - **The Appendix J audit reveals post-hoc key surgery.** Two task families required re-keying (138 of 249 originally-keyed couriers were already deactivated; a misweighted composite score) *after* runs were examined, with everything regraded and rerun. The transparency is admirable, but it raises the question the paper doesn't answer: how many keys would a truly independent auditor find, and should the audit be a living document rather than a one-time appendix? - **The injected-refund shortcut (Appendix J) weakens a headline fraud family.** All 664 anomalous refunds fall within the 98 simulator-injected storefronts, so "one pass over the refunds therefore finds every candidate" — the family tests ring-vs-control discrimination, not discovery. The authors keep it "as run" because fixing it "changes the world," but a benchmark paper should quantify how much easier the task became rather than leaving it to the appendix. - **Vendor authorship deserves a sentence.** All five authors are at TextQL, which sells data-agent products. title: I Don’t Always Do What I Am Told: The Case for Task Incongruence-Aware Systems for Technology-Supported Reflection on Social Interactions
authors: Chenxu Hao; Tiffany Matej Hrkalović; Bernd Dudzik; Hayley Hung
abstract: Technology-supported Self-Reflection (TSR) systems aim to facilitate learning through self-reflection. In the social domain, these systems often nudge individuals to perform better towards a certain outcome in a targeted task. Typically, this idea of support assumes that users pursue specific goals, which system creators anticipate will govern users’ behavior in targeted tasks. However, how goals shape behaviors in social interactions is complex: individuals’ goals can be highly idiosyncratic and multifaceted, sometimes contradictory to their best interest, and they are often not explicitly formulated in advance. We believe that viewing this complex landscape through the lens of a simple task formulation imposes limitations on the type of support these systems can provide. In this paper, we take a first step towards investigating the incongruence between assumed task goals and observed users’ behaviors and decisions in a partner selection setting, where participants need to select a partner for a cooperation task, and the apparent task goal can co-exist with other personal or relationship-oriented goals. First, we identify task-incongruent decisions, showing that even in a highly structured and incentivized setting, some choices deviate from the assumed task goal. Second, using a Large Language Model (LLM) to analyze conversational behavior, we explore topic-based and interactional indicators of task incongruence. Although the behavioral evidence is mixed, these findings still illustrate that what appears to be a reasonably assumed goal by the system may not be what users end up pursuing. In designing TSR systems, we believe that it is crucial to have capabilities for Task-Incongruence Awareness (TIA), enabling meaningful reflections on how users’ consciously or unconsciously self-ascribed goals are aligned with their behaviors and decisions.

title: Two pathways at once: An investigation of how reactance and ethicality shape student learning with AI
authors: Steven James Hyde; Andrew A. Hanna; Gundars Kaupins
source_name: The International Journal of Management Education
abstract: Generative AI tools promise to expand student agency in management education, yet the same tool can help and hurt learning inside a single classroom. We argue this contradiction is the signature of two psychological pathways running in parallel. Drawing on the cognitive-affective-conative framework, we develop a dual-pathway serial mediation model in which a cognitive pathway runs from psychological reactance through autonomy perceptions to effectiveness judgments, while an affective pathway runs from ethical perceptions through emotional engagement to effectiveness judgments. Ninety-seven undergraduate management students participated in two AI-enhanced activities with different chatbot tools across one semester. Both pathways operated as predicted. More surprising was how the cognitive pathway changed across exposures. At first use, reactance traveled through autonomy, consistent with self-determination theory. By the second activity, reactance bypassed autonomy and suppressed effectiveness directly. The affective pathway remained stable across exposures. For management educators, ethical framing before a student's first AI encounter may do more work than redesigning the tools themselves to preserve student choice. As a single-cohort study using two researcher-built chatbots, the results are preliminary and point to hypotheses for multi-site replication rather than population estimates.

title: An Integrated AI Platform for Accelerating Semiconductor Failure Analysis: Combining Similarity Search, Deep-Learning Image Retrieval, Automated Labeling, and Ontology-Guided Workflow Assistance
authors: Michael Beetz; Clemens Grünewald; Thomas Gänsler; Christian Burmer; Konstantin Schekotihin
source_name: Proceedings - International Symposium for Testing and Failure Analysis
abstract: Abstract Semiconductor failure analysis (FA) requires rapid access to relevant historical cases, consistent failure labeling, image-based pattern recognition, and methodologically correct investigation planning. In practice, these tasks are often supported by disconnected tools, leading to workflow friction and delayed root-cause identification. This paper presents AiFAct, an integrated, on-premise AI platform that supports the FA workflow end-to-end through six coordinated capabilities: multi-criteria similarity search with pair-specific reranking feedback, ontology-based automatic label prediction, quiz-based human verification for continuous model refinement, on-premise large language model (LLM) support for structured summaries and next-step proposals, deep-embedding image similarity for microscopy retrieval, and process-ontology-constrained workflow guidance. Unlike point solutions, the platform is designed as a closed feedback system where analyst interactions continuously improve ranking, labeling, and recommendation quality during routine work. In production-scale deployment across multi-site FA data, core candidate retrieval and reranking remains sub-second for candidate pools above 50,000 jobs, and analyst-facing query responses are delivered in under five seconds. The key contribution is workflow-level orchestration and feedback coupling rather than a single new standalone model. This architecture improves analyst trust through transparent scoring, supports knowledge transfer across sites, and preserves data sovereignty via fully on-premise operation.

title: AI Assistant Referral Traffic and Conversion Performance Relative to Organic Search: A 12-Month Multi-Site Benchmark, 2025-2026
authors: The SEO Works; Ben Foster
source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: A 12-month benchmark (September 2025 to August 2026) of referral traffic from AI assistants (ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini, Perplexity, Copilot and similar) compared with organic search, using Google Analytics 4 data from 95 websites (66 meeting volume thresholds; 63 with recorded organic conversions). Key findings: organic search delivered 39 times more sessions than AI assistants (2,825,594 versus 72,095). AI referrals equalled 2.6% of organic sessions. AI sessions converted 1.18x as well as organic search (7.18% versus 6.08%), with wide variation by customer type: B2C 1.51x, Mixed 1.46x, B2B Services 1.21x, B2B Products 0.62x. AI referral volume rose 36-39% across customer segments after ChatGPT began showing brands as clickable inline links in May 2026. Growth in AI referrals correlated with growth in organic traffic (r = +0.53 after controls); no support was found for a "billboard effect" on direct traffic. A 5% improvement in organic performance would add more conversions than doubling AI referral traffic. The record contains the paper (method, results, limitations) and the aggregated dataset with site identities removed and replaced by an index number and customer type. The web version is at https://www.seoworks.co.uk/downloads/ai-referral-traffic-benchmark/

title: Multi-Site Real-World Performance of Commercial AI for Pulmonary and Incidental Pulmonary Embolism Detection
authors: Aawez Mansuri; Mohammadreza Chavoshi; Theo Dapamede; Wasif Bala; Beatrice Brown-Mulry; Rohan Isaac; Bardia Khosravi; Hanzhou Li; Frank Li; John Timothy Moon; Chad Robichaux; Dan I. G. Cohen-Addad; Ninad V. Salastekar; Janice Newsome; Judy Wawira Gichoya; Hari Trivedi
abstract: Pulmonary embolism (PE) is a leading cause of cardiovascular mortality, yet the real-world performance of FDA-cleared AI detection models remains incompletely characterized. We retrospectively evaluated two FDA-cleared AI algorithms from a single commercial platform (Aidoc Medical BriefCase), one for PE triage on dedicated CT pulmonary angiography (CTPA; n = 30,678) and one for incidental PE (iPE) detection on routine contrast-enhanced CTs (n = 37,191), across a 17-facility academic health system. Reference-standard labels were extracted from radiology reports using a validated LLM pipeline (97% accuracy, kappa = 0.94). The PE model achieved 86.8% sensitivity and 99.1% specificity, with sensitivity declining from 99.3% for saddle emboli to 72.9% for subsegmental PE, and from 89.7% for acute to 65.3% for non-acute PE. The iPE model achieved 73.5% sensitivity and 99.8% specificity. Both models demonstrated lower sensitivity than FDA-clearance benchmarks while exceeding cleared specificity, with diminishing performance for peripheral and non-acute emboli mirroring known human reader limitations and underscoring the need for standardized post-market surveillance of AI-enabled medical devices.

title: Efficiency, Cost, and Quality: An Evaluation Framework for AI-Native Software Projects Measured in Tokens
authors: Wenchao Shi
source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Efficiency, Cost, and Quality: An Evaluation Framework for AI-Native Software Projects Measured in Tokens Author: Wenchao Shi Date: September 2026 Keywords: AI-native development, token accounting, evaluation framework, cost of quality, statistical process control, ISO 9001, COCOMO, evidence-based management Abstract AI-native software development delegates execution to large language model agents, and its dominant variable cost is billed computation measured in tokens. Projects nonetheless lack an evaluation framework that uses tokens as its unit of account and covers efficiency, cost, and quality together. This paper specifies such a framework. The unit of account is the session, measured in five token classes (input, output, reasoning, cache read, cache write) together with model identity and parent linkage. The data foundation consists of four attribution rules that close project membership and end in an explicit review queue rather than a guess, two audits that protect against over-broad exclusion and duplicate counting, three cost registers that must never be blended, and milestone segmentation with an additive conservation check. Evaluation then proceeds along three lines. Efficiency is defined as consumption per accepted increment, measured against the acceptance record rather than against activity, and is void when no such denominator exists. Cost is defined by register separation with exact reconciliation, because the estimated register usually dominates and a blended figure is not an accounting figure. Quality is defined by the composition of consumption rather than its quantity, using the classical division into prevention, appraisal, and failure, for which meta-work and recovery sessions are the AI-native analogues of scrap and rework. Each line carries a small indicator set with thresholds derived from observed cases. The framework's legitimacy is argued from the quality-management canon: goal-derived measurement, statistical process control, the cost-of-quality taxonomy, the process approach and process performance baselines of ISO 9001 and CMMI, lean waste analysis, effort-based cost models such as COCOMO, and the literature on metric pathologies. Governance rules, applicability boundaries, and a de-identified illustration from a fourteen-day embedded project (approximately 790 million tokens across four milestones) are provided, together with the conditions under which the framework should not be used at all. 摘要： AI 原生开发把执行交给大语言模型 Agent，其主导变动成本是以 token 计量的算力账单，但项目至今缺少一套以 token 为计量单位、同时覆盖效率、成本与质量的评估体系。本文给出这一体系：计量单位取会话中的五类 token 及模型身份与父会话指针；数据基础由四级归属规则、两项审计、三种费用口径与带守恒检查的里程碑分段构成；评估沿效率、成本、质量三条主线展开。效率以单位已交付增量的消耗为定义，分母来自验收记录，无分母则该主线不成立；成本以口径分列与精确对账为定义；质量以消耗的结构而非数量为定义，采用预防、鉴定、失效的经典分类，元工作与恢复会话即 AI 原生形态的废料与返工。体系的合法性依据来自质量管理体系的经典方法论，并附治理纪律、适用边界与一个去标识化实例。 Keywords: AI-native development; token accounting; evaluation framework; cost of quality; statistical process control; ISO 9001; COCOMO; evidence-based management 1. Introduction Software organisations have always estimated and controlled work through input measures: person-months, function points, story points, build minutes, cloud spend. Each survived because it is measurable, comparable inside a context, and actionable. AI-native development introduces an input measure that is simultaneously unusually precise and unusually opaque. Every model interaction is metered, and five token classes (input, output, reasoning, cache read, cache write) are counted by the serving infrastructure and stored per session. Yet no established framework says what those counts mean for a project. Three gaps follow, and they are the reason a framework rather than a metric is needed. Cost authorisation: the dominant variable cost is computation billed per token, and a figure without registers cannot support an authorisation decision. Capacity planning: token budgets constrain long-horizon projects much as headcount constrains traditional ones, and a team that cannot account for consumption cannot forecast. Quality visibility: a substantial share of consumption is rework, recovery, and meta-work such as searching history, rebuilding context, and retrying failed operations, and in the absence of a framework that consumption is recorded only as "expensive". This paper therefore specifies an evaluation framework measured in tokens. It is organised as frameworks are: a unit of account, a data foundation that makes the unit trustworthy, three evaluation lines with definitions and thresholds, governance rules for use, and explicit boundaries that state where the framework does not apply. The contribution is not a new statistic but a specification of what must be true before a token figure may be used to judge efficiency, cost, or quality. Two boundaries are fixed at the outset. The framework does not measure value, economic productivity, or individual performance; token consumption is an internal attribute of the development process, and the framework treats it as such. And its thresholds are baselines, in the process-performance sense, valid for the process that produced them until a broader sample contradicts them. 2. Criteria the framework must satisfy A framework that judges projects invites the objection that its measures are arbitrary. This section states the criteria the framework must meet, drawn from the quality-management canon, and each later design decision traces back to one of them. Measurement must be goal-derived. The goal-question-metric tradition introduced by Basili and Weiss and formalised by van Solingen and Berghout requires measures to descend from an explicit goal, through operational questions, to data; the order cannot be reversed. The framework's goal is not to reduce token consumption but to answer three questions: how much execution effort each increment consumed, whether that consumption was driven by identifiable disruptions, and how it was distributed across prevention, appraisal, and failure. Fenton and Pfleeger's distinction between internal and external attributes supplies the necessary modesty: tokens are directly observable internal attributes, whereas productivity and reliability are context-dependent external attributes, and treating the former as the latter is the specific error the framework exists to prevent. Process control precedes judgement. Shewhart's control charts and Deming's practice establish that a process metric is interpretable only when the process is in a state of statistical control, so that variation can be attributed to common causes inherent in the process rather than to sporadic assignable causes. A day of unusual consumption is therefore not a performance signal until the analyst asks whether a stable baseline exists and whether the excursion has an identifiable cause: a failed approach retried, a recovery session after lost context, or a classification error. Deming's warnings against managing by numbers alone and against driving fear into the system constrain use further: consumption data used to rank individuals converts a diagnostic instrument into a punitive one and produces the behaviour described below. Cost of quality has structure. Feigenbaum's total quality control and Juran's quality trilogy established that quality cost is not a single quantity but a structure: prevention, appraisal, and failure, with internal failure such as rework and external failure such as warranty loss. Crosby argued that prevention and appraisal spending displaces failure cost, and Taguchi generalised the point by treating any deviation from target as a loss. This taxonomy is the framework's interpretive core for quality, because it converts a scalar into a composition: tests written before implementation, contracts frozen in advance, and adversarial review by a separate delegated agent are prevention; executing the test matrix, reproducing defects, and verifying against gates are appraisal; retrying a failed approach, rebuilding a broken working state, and re-establishing context are failure. Meta-work is the AI-native analogue of scrap, because it consumes capacity to re-produce information that should have been preserved. Process approach, evidence-based decisions, and baselines. ISO 9001:2015 requires processes to be managed as interrelated activities with defined inputs, outputs, and performance indicators, monitored and measured, with decisions based on analysis of the resulting evidence; ISO/IEC/IEEE 15939 supplies the corresponding measurement process, from need definition through data collection to communication with uncertainty. CMMI's process performance concepts add the baseline: measured historical data about a process, used to predict and to judge whether a current result is normal. Two requirements follow for the framework: every reported figure must be traceable to source records, and uncertainty must be disclosed rather than hidden. Lean waste and Six Sigma sequence. Lean treats waste as activity that consumes resources without creating value: waiting, over-processing, defects, work in progress. Token accounting maps onto this list directly, with waiting visible as sessions stalled on unavailable resources, over-processing as repeated verification of the same artifact, defects as regression-driven rework, and work in progress as half-finished artifacts whose context must be rebuilt. Six Sigma contributes sequence rather than apparatus: measure before analysing, analyse before improving, and institutionalise control so that improvement persists. Effort-based cost models and outcome critiques. Introduction Software organisations have always estimated and controlled work through input measures: person-months, function points, story points, build minutes, cloud spend. Each survived because it is measurable, comparable inside a context, and actionable. AI-native development introduces an input measure that is simultaneously unusually precise and unusually opaque. Every model interaction is metered, and five token classes (input, output, reasoning, cache read, cache write) are counted by the serving infrastructure and stored per session. Yet no established framework says what those counts mean for a project. Three gaps follow, and they are the reason a framework rather than a metric is needed. Cost authorisation: the dominant variable cost is computation billed per token, and a figure without registers cannot support an authorisation decision. Capacity planning: token budgets constrain long-horizon projects much as headcount constrains traditional ones, and a team that cannot account for consumption cannot forecast. Quality visibility: a substantial share of consumption is rework, recovery, and meta-work such as searching history, rebuilding context, and retrying failed operations, and in the absence of a framework that consumption is recorded only as \"expensive\". This paper therefore specifies an evaluation framework measured in tokens. It is organised as frameworks are: a unit of account, a data foundation that makes the unit trustworthy, three evaluation lines with definitions and thresholds, governance rules for use, and explicit boundaries that state where the framework does not apply. The contribution is not a new statistic but a specification of what must be true before a token figure may be used to judge efficiency, cost, or quality. Two boundaries are fixed at the outset. The framework does not measure value, economic productivity, or individual performance; token consumption is an internal attribute of the development process, and the framework treats it as such. And its thresholds are baselines, in the process-performance sense, valid for the process that produced them until a broader sample contradicts them. 2. Criteria the framework must satisfy A framework that judges projects invites the objection that its measures are arbitrary. This section states the criteria the framework must meet, drawn from the quality-management canon, and each later design decision traces back to one of them. Measurement must be goal-derived. The goal-question-metric tradition introduced by Basili and Weiss and formalised by van Solingen and Berghout requires measures to descend from an explicit goal, through operational questions, to data; the order cannot be reversed. Cost of quality has structure. title: Teaching LLMs to Generate Challenging MILP Instances via Solver Feedback
authors: Jitin Singla; Parikshit Pareek; Pratik Jawanpuria; Parag Singla
abstract: Generating optimization instances that are both feasible and computationally challenging is crucial for benchmarking solvers and training learning-based optimization algorithms. Existing non-LLM generators rely on seed instances or parameter tuning, resulting in high test-time computational cost, while existing LLM generators lack explicit hardness measures. Recent reinforcement learning methods with verifier feedback evaluate only binary correctness, which is misaligned with generating challenging problems. We note that an optimization solver reports the cost of solving at several stages of its pipeline, and leverage this to design a reward that scores both the solvability and the hardness of generated problems, measured by branch-and-bound nodes and post-cut relaxation gaps. Our key idea is a challenger-solver asymmetric self-play approach, where an LLM challenger generates progressively harder instances and the solver verifies feasibility and hardness, so no seed or training MILP instances are required. We fine-tune Gemma-4-12B and Qwen3.5-4B with GRPO and a size curriculum into OptiScribe-12B and OptiScribe-4B, which generate feasible yet challenging MILP problems from natural language instructions. On capacitated facility location and max-cut, OptiScribe-12B raises median SCIP search nodes by 1.7-5x and post-cut gaps by 1.1-1.7x over its base model and improves the feasibility rate on facility location by 9-19 points, while OptiScribe-4B raises median nodes by up to 15.6x. The problems cover a wider difficulty range than public benchmarks of the same size, follow instructions on density and difficulty, and can tune solver settings for families that public libraries lack. These results indicate that optimization-specific rewards, used in self-play mode, can teach LLMs to generate high-difficulty optimization benchmarks. We will release our code and models publicly on acceptance.

Keywords: AI-native development; token accounting; evaluation framework; cost of quality; statistical process control; ISO 9001; COCOMO; evidence-based management 1. Introduction Software organisations have always estimated and controlled work through input measures: person-months, function points, story points, build minutes, cloud spend. Each survived because it is measurable, comparable inside a context, and actionable. AI-native development introduces an input measure that is simultaneously unusually precise and unusually opaque. Every model interaction is metered, and five token classes (input, output, reasoning, cache read, cache write) are counted by the serving infrastructure and stored per session. Yet no established framework says what those counts mean for a project. Three gaps follow, and they are the reason a framework rather than a metric is needed. Cost authorisation: the dominant variable cost is computation billed per token, and a figure without registers cannot support an authorisation decision. Capacity planning: token budgets constrain long-horizon projects much as headcount constrains traditional ones, and a team that cannot account for consumption cannot forecast. Quality visibility: a substantial share of consumption is rework, recovery, and meta-work such as searching history, rebuilding context, and retrying failed operations, and in the absence of a framework that consumption is recorded only as \"expensive\". This paper therefore specifies an evaluation framework measured in tokens. It is organised as frameworks are: a unit of account, a data foundation that makes the unit trustworthy, three evaluation lines with definitions and thresholds, governance rules for use, and explicit boundaries that state where the framework does not apply. The contribution is not a new statistic but a specification of what must be true before a token figure may be used to judge efficiency, cost, or quality. Two boundaries are fixed at the outset. The framework does not measure value, economic productivity, or individual performance; token consumption is an internal attribute of the development process, and the framework treats it as such. And its thresholds are baselines, in the process-performance sense, valid for the process that produced them until a broader sample contradicts them. 2. Criteria the framework must satisfy A framework that judges projects invites the objection that its measures are arbitrary. This section states the criteria the framework must meet, drawn from the quality-management canon, and each later design decision traces back to one of them. Measurement must be goal-derived. The goal-question-metric tradition introduced by Basili and Weiss and formalised by van Solingen and Berghout requires measures to descend from an explicit goal, through operational questions, to data; the order cannot be reversed. The framework's goal is not to reduce token consumption but to answer three questions: how much execution effort each increment consumed, whether that consumption was driven by identifiable disruptions, and how it was distributed across prevention, appraisal, and failure. Fenton and Pfleeger's distinction between internal and external attributes supplies the necessary modesty: tokens are directly observable internal attributes, whereas productivity and reliability are context-dependent external attributes, and treating the former as the latter is the specific error the framework exists to prevent. Process control precedes judgement. Shewhart's control charts and Deming's practice establish that a process metric is interpretable only when the process is in a state of statistical control, so that variation can be attributed to common causes inherent in the process rather than to sporadic assignable causes. A day of unusual consumption is therefore not a performance signal until the analyst asks whether a stable baseline exists and whether the excursion has an identifiable cause: a failed approach retried, a recovery session after lost context, or a classification error. Deming's warnings against managing by numbers alone and against driving fear into the system constrain use further: consumption data used to rank individuals converts a diagnostic instrument into a punitive one and produces the behaviour described below. Cost of quality has structure. Feigenbaum's total quality control and Juran's quality trilogy established that quality cost is not a single quantity but a structure: prevention, appraisal, and failure, with internal failure such as rework and external failure such as warranty loss. Crosby argued that prevention and appraisal spending displaces failure cost, and Taguchi generalised the point by treating any deviation from target as a loss. This taxonomy is the framework's interpretive core for quality, because it converts a scalar into a composition: tests written before implementation, contracts frozen in advance, and adversarial review by a separate delegated agent are prevention; executing the test matrix, reproducing defects, and verifying against gates are appraisal; retrying a failed approach, rebuilding a broken working state, and re-establishing context are failure. Meta-work is the AI-native analogue of scrap, because it consumes capacity to re-produce information that should have been preserved. Process approach, evidence-based decisions, and baselines. ISO 9001:2015 requires processes to be managed as interrelated activities with defined inputs, outputs, and performance indicators, monitored and measured, with decisions based on analysis of the resulting evidence; ISO\/IEC\/IEEE 15939 supplies the corresponding measurement process, from need definition through data collection to communication with uncertainty. CMMI's process performance concepts add the baseline: measured historical data about a process, used to predict and to judge whether a current result is normal. Two requirements follow for the framework: every reported figure must be traceable to source records, and uncertainty must be disclosed rather than hidden. Lean waste and Six Sigma sequence. Lean treats waste as activity that consumes resources without creating value: waiting, over-processing, defects, work in progress. Token accounting maps onto this list directly, with waiting visible as sessions stalled on unavailable resources, over-processing as repeated verification of the same artifact, defects as regression-driven rework, and work in progress as half-finished artifacts whose context must be rebuilt. Six Sigma contributes sequence rather than apparatus: measure before analysing, analyse before improving, and institutionalise control so that improvement persists. title: Weaver: A System for AI-RAN Compute Sharing with Foundation Model Training
authors: Leyang Xue; Tianxin Wang; Xin Zhe Khooi; Jiaxun Yang; Dheeraj Mahendiran; Yufeng Xia; Mun Choon Chan; Myungjin Lee; Mahesh K. Marina
abstract: The emergence of AI-RAN infrastructure, which equips cell sites with GPU-accelerated hardware, creates an opportunity to colocate non-RAN workloads with primary RAN processing. We explore using this spare capacity for decentralized training of foundation models (FMs), one of the most compute-intensive AI workloads. We present the first characterization of spare GPU capacity in AI-RAN systems at both micro-scale--across transmission slots within a cell site--and macro-scale--across sites. Our analysis finds that 40-85% of GPU capacity is unused; although this capacity is temporally bursty at individual sites, it is spatially complementary across sites. To safely and efficiently harness these resources, we present Weaver, a system that opportunistically trains FMs alongside latency-critical RAN workloads without degrading RAN performance. Weaver adopts a RAN-first design: a spare-compute controller integrated into the MAC scheduler uses compute-aware scheduling to smooth RAN GPU demand and exposes more usable spare GPU capacity. A two-level elastic training framework then adapts to dynamic, heterogeneous spare capacity within and across sites. Experiments on an O-RAN-aligned system prototype show that Weaver creates up to 4.9x more usable spare compute and utilizes up to 83% of the available spare capacity. On a multi-site testbed, Weaver improves training throughput by 2.1-3.7x over baseline approaches.

title: MINT: Modeling GenAI Impact on Network Traffic
authors: Andrew Nguyen; Samson Kempiak; Agrim Gupta; Koushik Kar; Ish Kumar Jain
abstract: Generative AI (GenAI) is becoming a mainstream network workload, yet packet-level simulators lack measure\-ment-driven GenAI traffic models. Currently researchers must approximate GenAI services using traditional sources such as file transfer and video streaming, limiting realistic network evaluation of scheduling and capacity planning. We present MINT, a measurement and modeling framework for GenAI network traffic. Using an isolated net\-work-namespace capture pipeline, we collect client-side traces from three LLM providers across four modalities, cloud and edge servers, and wired and wireless network access points. We find that GenAI modalities exhibit distinct upload/download asymmetry and burst structures that differ from traditional applications. MINT clusters and models these burst regimes and validate empirical burst timing distribution behavior in ns-3 with normalized Wasserstein distances of 2--25\%. Our results also reveal that realistic packet bursts have significantly more variability than constant token generator models. MINT open-sources the first measurement-driven GenAI traffic model for packet-level network simulation.

title: A non-destructive methodological framework for modernizing legacy clinical reporting systems for AI-driven pharmacoinformatics: a SAS case study
authors: Jaime Yan
abstract: Legacy clinical reporting pipelines bottleneck drug development and pharmacovigilance: they encode regulatory-grade analytical logic but produce opaque output with no machine-readable intermediate layer, resisting integration with artificial intelligence (AI). Existing modernization approaches force a choice between full rewrites that abandon validated logic and incremental refactoring that preserves structural barriers to AI access. We present a non-destructive framework that achieves AI-driven pharmacoinformatics readiness without altering legacy source code. A metadata layer — a bridge map, a typed Intermediate Representation (IR), and an orchestrator — wraps existing reporting components, re-exposes their outputs as structured data consumable by large language models (LLMs), and enables optional incremental consolidation of selected components while the remainder operates unchanged. On a 558-component industrial SAS reporting library (373,000 lines of code), the framework demonstrated immediate AI readiness under coexistence mode with the legacy library unchanged. Where consolidation was elected, the modernized core achieved a 92% reduction in consolidated-core SAS lines of code (excluding the Python and YAML layers). Parity validation on 14 report types from an internal Phase III study cleared an 80% cell-level triage-admission gate on 11 of 14 reports (mean across all 14 report types 82.7%, best 99.2%); the three remaining reports differed in table-layout geometry rather than in computed values. A public benchmark on CDISC CDISCPilot01 data achieved 100% regression-consistency against frozen reference outputs across 5 reports (4,764 cells, 0 mismatches) — a reproducibility benchmark rather than independent validation. In a proof-of-concept study with a single large language model, the IR illustrated the feasibility of table summarization, adverse-event anomaly detection (a pharmacovigilance signal-detection example), and trial configuration generation — feasibility rather than validated performance. The framework offers a regulation-aware path to AI-integrated clinical trial reporting intended to reduce modernization overhead without interrupting ongoing regulatory submissions. Its regulatory-traceability features are design properties rather than validated compliance: no formal Installation/Operational/Performance Qualification (IQ/OQ/PQ) has been performed. All results derive from a single case study; the methodology is designed to be reusable across organizations and library scales, pending multi-site empirical validation.

title: Beyond Tool Use: Accountable Scholarly Augmentation, Responsible AI Literacy, and Publication Readiness Among Emerging Scholars
authors: Sana Hussan
abstract: Generative artificial intelligence (GenAI) is rapidly transforming postgraduate research communication, creating opportunities for academic assistance while also posing risks to source authenticity and intellectual stewardship. Based on an empirical multi-site meta-synthesis of N=4,280 doctoral and early-career researchers across eight major universities, this study establishes and validates the Accountable Scholarly Augmentation framework. Findings show GenAI effectively supports low-level tasks like outlining and stylistic framing. However, unguided use creates an "Overconfidence Gap," where high prose fluency masks factual errors and citation hallucinations (up to 38.2% unverified claims). Multivariate analysis reveals that punitive policy warnings fail to reduce manuscript defects. Conversely, integrated responsible AI programs significantly decrease pre-submission desk rejections from 41.8% to 12.6% (β=.52,p<.001). The study emphasizes shifting research integrity governance and graduate education from punitive policy enforcement to a developmental publication-readiness framework.

title: PulseAir: rigor-first evaluation of wearable air-quality forecasting
authors: Md All Shahria; Sanjeda Dewan Mithila; Anik Sarker Rudro; Irfanul Islam Payel
source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Research code for a thesis on wearable air-quality forecasting for an ESP32 neckband. The pipeline covers preprocessing with imputation provenance, CTGAN and SMOTE augmentation with a paired-bootstrap ablation, LSTM/Transformer sequence models with MC-dropout uncertainty, Mondrian conformal prediction, SHAP attribution, an LLM risk advisory with validated output, and compression and ONNX export for edge deployment. Its central contribution is evaluation discipline: every headline metric is reported against a zero-parameter persistence floor, single-split results are re-tested with rolling-origin cross-validation, and interventions that raise an aggregate metric while degrading a safety-critical class are disqualified. Applied to the UCI Beijing multi-site data, that discipline shows no model reliably beats persistence at a six-hour horizon; the deployable result and the validated advisory-class result both come from Bangladesh data, the wearable's target population.

title: Empowering Hybrid Attention Models on NPUs
authors: Yinyuan Zhang; Daliang Xu; Xiaolong Huang; Wangsong Yin; Yun Ma; Mengwei Xu; Gang Huang
abstract: Hybrid attention models have emerged as a crucial architecture for Large Language Models (LLMs) (e.g., the Qwen3.5 and Kimi series). Their memory and computational efficiency make them highly attractive for on-device inference, forming a promising synergy with edge Neural Processing Units (NPUs). However, naive execution of these hybrid models on edge NPUs fails to deliver these benefits, often bottlenecking the prefill stage due to severe memory-system inefficiencies and architectural mismatches within the linear attention (LA) layers. We present HA-NPU, the first system to enable efficient hybrid attention LLM inference on edge NPUs without modifying the underlying algorithms. HA-NPU enhances execution efficiency by reorganizing the dataflow of the LA components across three levels: (1) At the core level, it partitions workloads by the head dimension and fuses dependent operators, eliminating cross-core global memory accesses; (2) At the operator level, it reorders execution to consume intermediate tensors immediately, drastically minimizing local-buffer pressure; (3) At the tensor level, it employs dataflow-aware layout planning to minimize transformation overhead between matrix and vector processing units. Compared to competitive baselines, HA-NPU achieves up to 35.95$\times$ LA kernel speedup and 36.14$\times$ energy reduction, delivering up to 2.03$\times$ faster end-to-end request latency. The source code will be made publicly available at https://github.com/yinyuanzhang/HA-NPU

title: Multimodal LLMs Outperform Pathology Foundation Models in Cross-Domain Histological Similarity
authors: Yishu Zhang; Yun Li; Daiwei Zhang
abstract: State-of-the-art pathology foundation models, trained on millions of histology tiles, can fail to preserve tissue similarity when comparisons cross slide or institution boundaries. We show that general-purpose multimodal LLMs, without being trained as pathology foundation models, consistently outperform these specialized models in cross-domain histological similarity judgments. Using a relative similarity framework that we release as the MOSAIC (Model Similarity Assessment across Institutions and Cohorts) benchmark, we evaluate 17 models across 6 datasets and find that pathology encoders often rank same-institution, different-disease tiles as more similar than same-disease, different-institution tiles, a clinically dangerous failure mode invisible to standard within-domain evaluations. LLMs appear less susceptible to this failure, likely because they perform semantic visual comparison of morphology and tissue architecture rather than relying on shortcut features tied to acquisition context. Scaling training data does not resolve the problem for pathology encoders, implicating the learning objective rather than data coverage. Our results expose a fundamental robustness gap in current pathology foundation models and establish multimodal LLMs as a viable alternative for cross-institutional retrieval, dataset harmonization, and multi-site quality control. Code and data will be released upon acceptance.

title: STEMBench: an Inspect-AI benchmark harness for research-grade STEM agent tasks
authors: Anonymous
source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: A benchmark harness for evaluating LLM agents on research-grade STEM tasks, built on Inspect AI. Each task is a self-contained contract folder that the harness loads, stages into a sandbox, runs through an agent, and scores without task-specific harness code. WHAT THIS ARCHIVE CONTAINS Harness source code: task loading, Inspect task/solver construction, tool surface (bash, python, data exploration, literature search, document reading, submission validation), Docker and local sandbox backends, scorers, and the CLI entry points for running, grading, and aggregating. The complete contract for 12 tasks across three domains — astrophysics (simulated and real Stokes inversion, PLAsTiCC light-curve classification), high-energy physics (top-quark tagging, HiggsML uncertainty quantification, LHC Olympics anomaly detection, DarkMachines anomaly detection), and neuroscience (ABIDE multi-site diagnosis and age prediction, resting-state BOLD HRF deconvolution, neural-mass model family classification, parameter recovery, and digital twins). Per task: the agent-facing task statement, the scoring definition, the grader, per-file SHA-256 checksums, a literature index citing sources by DOI, baseline and expert reference solutions, and dataset-generation code where the payload is synthetic. Leaderboards and the per-run report used for the reported results, plus the campaign script that records the exact model, agent, sandbox, reasoning effort, and budget limits behind them. WHAT IT DOES NOT CONTAIN Dataset payloads are not in this archive. They are published as a companion dataset record, https://doi.org/10.5281/zenodo.22960135, as one archive per task, each unpacking at this repository's root. Every task ships per-file SHA-256 checksums so any copy can be verified byte-for-byte. Without the payloads the harness can be inspected and extended, but tasks cannot be executed or scored. Evaluation run logs (.eval files) are not published. The reported scores are in LEADERBOARD.md, the per-task CSVs under leaderboards/, and report.html, which embeds the per-run agent trajectories. One task's payload (ABIDE-derived) is never redistributed: its source data is CC-BY-NC-SA and derives from human neuroimaging data. A preparation script rebuilds it locally from the source archive and verifies the result against the published checksums. Published reference papers are not redistributed. Every external reference is cited by DOI with title, authors, venue, and a resolvable link. REPRODUCIBILITY REPRODUCING.md is the step-by-step checklist. Two limits are stated up front: reported scores come from hosted preview model snapshots run without a fixed seed or temperature, so they are samples from a distribution rather than bit-reproducible values; and dependency versions are not pinned in this version of the archive. DATA_LICENSES.md records the provenance and licence of every task's data, including the attribution notices required by the CC-BY-4.0 sources. LICENCE Code, task contracts, graders, reference solutions, and documentation are MIT. Task descriptions and the synthetic data payloads are CC-BY-4.0 and are covered by the companion dataset record.

title: A Standardized Protocol for Fear Extinction Enhancement Research
authors: M. Alexandra Kredlow; Meghan Whalen; Patrick A.F. Laing; Lingwei Ouyang; August C. Morgan; Samuel Emerson Cooper; Bram Vervliet; Joseph E. Dunsmoor
abstract: For over a century, fear conditioning and extinction have served as a foundational model and laboratory protocol for studying how fear is learned and regulated in health and disorder. Several recent innovations in exposure treatments for anxiety-related psychopathology follow advances in fear extinction research. However, the field lacks a standardized protocol—critical given the many consequential parameters in conditioning protocols—that provides a benchmark standard for systematic research on how to improve exposure via enhanced extinction. Here, we present a standardized differential fear conditioning protocol based on international expert input via survey and initial multi-site validation data (n=196; 65% female). The protocol demonstrates expected patterns of fear acquisition and sufficient extinction and return of fear response needed for tests of enhanced extinction. The protocol is simple to implement and amenable to modification, providing an accessible tool for both field-domain experts and allied fields with interest in fear and anxiety.

title: A governed framework combining large language models and human oversight for supplier selection
authors: Mohammad Reza Rezaei; Sridhar Sreemulnath Iyer; Omid Fatahi Valilai
abstract: Supplier selection requires organisations to combine structured procurement records with evolving information on sustainability, compliance, operational risk, and market conditions. The ability to reassess suppliers as this information changes is important for maintaining responsive and resilient supply chains. This paper proposes a governed human-in-the-loop framework that connects procurement intent, supplier data, qualitative evidence, multi-criteria analysis, explanation, and managerial review. Language model components support the interpretation of sourcing requests, the extraction of source-linked evidence, and the formulation of revised decision scenarios. Deterministic services remain responsible for weighting, constraint application, scoring, and ranking, while procurement professionals approve consequential analytical and evidential choices. Partial automation of evidence processing and scenario preparation allows supplier evaluations to be updated in response to changing conditions while procurement professionals retain final decision authority. The framework is examined using public procurement records and controlled benchmarks covering scenario formulation, evidence processing, multi-criteria trade-offs, robustness, and explanation fidelity. Its design incorporates schema validation, source-level provenance, explicit evidence policies, deterministic fallbacks, and four human approval checkpoints. Using the extended procurement-fit representation increases Ref@ 10 from 5.259% to 31.642%; the language model components achieve a valid structured-output rate of 1.000, mean evidence-claim F1 of 0.928, and exact preservation of the fixed deterministic ranking in all explanation cases. The study contributes an auditable approach to combining the interpretive capabilities of language models with established supplier-selection methods, providing a basis for more adaptive supplier evaluation while recognising the need for validation in enterprise procurement settings.

title: PROSPECTS FOR THE DEVELOPMENT OF BUILT-IN INTELLIGENT DIAGNOSTIC SYSTEMS FOR AGRICULTURAL MACHINERY
authors: A.S. SAYAPIN; M.N. KOSTOMAKHIN; E.V. PESTRYAKOV
abstract: The state of the agricultural machinery park in Russia is characterized by significant wear: more than 57 percent of tractors have a service life of more than 10 years, the annual growth of the park is only 6.4 percent of the number of equipment requiring disposal, repair costs have increased by more than 30 percent over the past three years for 80 percent of farms, which exacerbates the financial burden on agricultural producers and poses a threat to the technological sovereignty of the agro-industrial complex. (Research purpose) The research purpose is conducting a comprehensive analysis of the prospects for the development of built-in intelligent diagnostic systems of agricultural machines, taking into account the current state of the fleet of equipment and identifying ways of their effective implementation in domestic agriculture. (Materials and methods) We performed a systematic analysis of the state of the agricultural machinery park using the monographic method, statistical analysis of survey data of agricultural enterprises from more than 60 subjects of the Russian Federation, analysis of existing solutions in the field of digital diagnostics of agricultural machinery and prospects for the use of large language models. (Results and discussion) It was found that the transition from reactive to predictive diagnostics reduces unscheduled downtime by 35-45 percent and reduces repair costs by 25-30 percent. It was shown that the use of artificial neural networks to analyze the parameters of the technical state provides prediction of failures with high accuracy. We proposed the concept of remote diagnostics based on large language models and cloud-based AI services based on the "diagnostics as a service" model, which allows small farms to access expert knowledge without significant capital investments. (Conclusions) The introduction of built-in intelligent diagnostic systems is a necessary condition for the technical re-equipment of the agro-industrial complex of Russia, but state support measures are required, including subsidies for the purchase of diagnostic equipment. Satellite communication is proposed for monitoring the technical condition and intelligent diagnostics.

title: Accelerating metadata annotation in collaborative research centers: A hybrid AI workflow for biomedical entities
authors: Manuel Watter; Felix Engel; Aref Kalantari; Claudia Giuliani; Karin Schuller; Claus-Werner Franzke; Markus Sperandio; Harald Binder; Klaus Kaier
abstract: Abstract Background Collaborative Research Centers rely on FAIR-compliant, richly structured metadata, yet manual annotation is a major bottleneck. We implemented a search-augmented large language model (LLM) workflow within a local research data management system to pre-annotate biomedical entities, using human-in-the-loop verification to ensure data quality. Methods The pipeline uses Gemini 3 Pro in a two-step prompting strategy: (1) identify dataset deposits and stable identifiers in articles converted to Markdown; (2) extract structured fields from curated repository landing pages rendered via a headless browser. To handle a highly hierarchical metadata schema, we flattened the schema for prompting and remapped outputs to strict JSON with granular provenance tags. Authors received pre-filled metadata and could accept, edit, or delete entries (TP, FP, FN mapping). Performance metrics (precision, recall, F1) were estimated as proportions and synthesized via random-effects meta-analysis. Results Among 51 screened articles, the LLM identified a repository deposit in 31; authors responded for 17 (55% of articles with an identified deposit; 33% of all screened articles), yielding 39 verified datasets. False positives were rare (mean 0.23) and false negatives low (mean 1.46). Precision was consistently high at 99.65% (95% CI 98.42%–100.00%). Recall showed more variability at 93.75% (95% CI 89.79%–96.96%), and the F1 score reached 96.17% (95% CI 93.78%–98.11%). Conclusions The hybrid workflow achieved high author-verified precision with moderate recall, shifting effort from drafting to reviewing while maintaining schema compliance. As these metrics rely on author acceptance and response rates were modest, broader, multi-site validation is needed.

title: Enhancing Near-Real-Time Amazon Forest Monitoring Using GeoAI: A Case Study on Selective Logging — companion reproducibility data
authors: Evandro Taquary; Guilherme Mataveli; Sérgio Nogueira; Daniel Braga; Gilberto Ribeiro de Queiroz; Luiz E. O. C. Aragão

abstract: This record contains the companion data for the paper Enhancing Near-Real-Time Amazon Forest Monitoring Using GeoAI: A Case Study on Selective Logging. It is organised into seven categories: the pretraining corpus for the spatiotemporal masked-autoencoder foundation model; the labelled dataset the downstream model is trained and cross-validated on; small reference-data files: the interpreter annotations the soft labels are derived from (annotations.json), the alert view dates that close each monitoring period (its end_period), and the downstream model's cached out-of-fold scores; the foundation-model checkpoint; the downstream model's checkpoints (20 leave-one-out cross-validation folds); the visual-interpretation panels the annotators read when placing the reference dates, one per marked observation and per monitoring reference, with a manifest (added in version 1.1.0); and the outputs of the detector evaluation: the nested leave-one-MU-out evaluation of the detector grid search, the negative test on the 51 interpreter-certified logging-free observations never used in training, and the survey of DETER alerts inside each analysed period (added in version 1.1.0).
