title: Automated Phenotypic Characterization in Rare Hematologic Malignancies Using a Large Language Model–Based Framework
authors: Muhammad Ali Khan; Umair Ayub; Salman Ayub Jajja; Muhammad Umair Anjum; Kainat Warraich; Prateek Jain; Japneet Kaur Oberoi; Mousab Al Abbas; Muhammad Hussnain Sadiq; Muhammad Uzair Sarfraz; Ziyi Huang; Irbaz Bin Riaz; Jeanne M. Palmer
abstract: Abstract Background Diagnosis and risk stratification in rare hematologic malignancies such as myeloproliferative neoplasms (MPNs) – polycythemia vera (PV), essential thrombocythemia (ET), and myelofibrosis (MF) – require expert review of longitudinal, heterogeneous clinical records. This process is cognitively demanding, inconsistently applied, and difficult to scale beyond tertiary centers. No automated phenotyping workflow currently exists for hematologic malignancies. Methods A HIPAA-compliant large language model (LLM) framework for phenotyping MPN was developed to integrate (i) rule-based retrieval of bone marrow biopsy reports, clinical notes, and structured laboratory results from the electronic health record (EHR); (ii) zero-shot extraction of diagnostic and prognostic variables from unstructured text using GPT-4 Turbo; (iii) a clinician-informed source-prioritization algorithm to reconcile conflicting multi-source data; (iv) WHO/ICC-criteria–based diagnostic classification; and (v) NCCN-based risk stratification using the conventional risk model for PV, IPSET-thrombosis for ET, and DIPSS, DIPSS-plus, and MIPSS70/MIPSS70+ v2 for MF. Patients were identified via MPN-related ICD-9/10 codes; cases met 2017 WHO criteria or had a hematologist-documented diagnosis, and controls did not. The cohort was split into a prompt-development set (n = 60) and a held-out test set (n = 450; 75 cases and 75 controls per disease). Ground truth was established by independent dual-clinician chart review with consensus adjudication. LLM performance was evaluated against the ground truth: variable-level extraction using accuracy, F1 score, and Cohen’s kappa; patient-level diagnostic classification using sensitivity, specificity, and Cohen’s kappa; and prognostic risk stratification (among confirmed cases) using accuracy, weighted F1 score, and quadratic-weighted Cohen’s kappa. Wilson 95% confidence intervals (CIs) were used for proportions and bootstrap 95% CIs with 500 resamples for F1 scores. Results The held-out test set included 450 patients (PV: 150; ET: 150; MF: 150) with pathology reports and structured laboratory results, and 172 patients (PV: 52; ET: 55; MF: 65) with clinical notes. From pathology reports, overall variable extraction accuracy and F1 score were 99% (95% CI, 98–100) and 1.00 (0.99–1.00) for PV, 100% (99–100) and 0.99 (0.96–1.00) for ET, and 100% (99–100) and 0.99 (0.97–1.00) for MF. From clinical notes, overall accuracy and F1 score were 96% (91–100) and 0.94 (0.85–1.00) for PV, 100% (100–100) and 1.00 (1.00–1.00) for ET, and 100% (99–100) and 0.98 (0.95–1.00) for MF. Diagnostic sensitivity was 100% (95% CI, 95.1–100.0) for PV, ET, and MF; specificity was 98.7% (92.8–99.8) for PV and 100% (95.1–100.0) for both ET and MF, with Cohen’s kappa of 0.99 for PV and 1.00 for ET and MF. Risk stratification accuracy was 100% with weighted F1 score of 1.00 and quadratic-weighted Cohen’s kappa of 1.00 across all three diseases. A pre-specified source-ablation analysis showed that pathology reports alone were sufficient for diagnosis (sensitivity 98.7% for PV, 100% for ET, 96.0% for MF; specificity 100% across all three subtypes) but inadequate for prognostication (accuracy 69.3% for PV, 93.3% for ET, 77.3% for MF). Adding clinical notes to pathology reports recovered full prognostic accuracy of 100% across all three diseases. Conclusions This first-in-class automated framework achieved expert-level performance for MPN diagnosis and risk stratification from real-world EHR data, establishing a foundation for scalable, standardized phenotyping in rare hematologic malignancies. Prospective, multi-site validation is warranted before clinical deployment.

title: The Proofload Method: Constrained-Context Delivery with Stateless AI Agents
authors: Housseyn Guettaf
source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: AI coding agents are increasingly deployed with broad autonomy over large contexts. In systems whose correctness depends on cross-module guarantees, such as regulated event-driven platforms and broker libraries over external protocols, the properties that matter most are not local to any file an agent edits: idempotent effects, ordered consumption, erasure against statutory retention, audit completeness, capability claims. The Proofload Method restricts agent scope instead of extending it. Work proceeds through a staged pipeline of typed artifacts, and agents implement only inside reviewed handoffs. Four mechanisms keep the artifact corpus in agreement: per-slice freezing of contracts over typed ports and single-producer events; a mechanical consistency checker that fails the build on cross-artifact drift and grows by promoting recurring defect classes to rules; immutable adversarial review records; and a status ledger restricted to claims backed by named evidence. The method is accompanied by working hypotheses grounded in known properties of large language models, a reference implementation with a worked example and a mutation-tested checker, and observations from two instantiations: a confidential greenfield build, and a public refounding of an agent-built Redis Streams library. The cases provide feasibility evidence and a bounded brownfield observation; controlled evaluation remains future work.

title: A Conceptual Study for Cognitive Bias Amplification in Agentic AI-Driven Business Processes, Management, and Intelligence
authors: Subhra R. Mondal; Subhankar Das; Vasiliki G. Vrana
abstract: Agentic artificial intelligence (AAI) and retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) are increasingly embedded in organisational business intelligence (BI) and business process management (BPM). Unlike conventional AI, these systems set sub-goals, plan multi-step workflows, and retrieve and store information under limited human supervision. This article argues that such autonomy not only transmits human cognitive bias into organisational decisions but also amplifies that bias under identifiable conditions. We develop the Bias Amplification Model (BAM), a three-layer account of how bias enters and escalates. In the injection layer, human biases enter through goal framing, prompt design, and data scoping. In the propagation layer, the agent compounds these biases across autonomous execution steps. In the crystallisation layer, RAG memory encodes biassed outputs as retrievable organisational knowledge that later cycles treat as evidence. A feedback loop links the three layers, converting episodic human bias into structural organisational bias. We state seven propositions, specify amplifying and mitigating conditions, and ground the model in a PRISMA-guided synthesis of 47 studies. A controlled, replicated experiment with an autonomous agent in a supplier-selection pipeline provides initial empirical support for injection, propagation, the mitigating effect of a single governance checkpoint, and bias transmission across a task boundary via retrieved memory. The framework reframes AI-driven process optimisation as a possible source of silent decline in decision quality.

title: Sequential multi-site fine-tuning for incremental deployment of large language models for mobility functional status extraction
authors: Xingyi Liu; Muskan Garg; Eunji Jeon; Heling Jia; Cynthia S. Crowson; Jennifer L. St. Sauver; Sandeep R. Pagali; Sunghwan Sohn
abstract: Objective: This study evaluated sequential multi-site fine-tuning of large language models (LLMs), simulating incremental deployment across institutions for extracting mobility functional status from unstructured clinical notes. Materials and Methods: We assembled a corpus of 600 clinical notes from 3 institutions, yielding 3810 annotated note sections (1200 training; 2610 testing). Building upon our previously established LLM mobility extraction pipeline, which utilized optimized prompt engineering, we applied parameter-efficient low-rank adaptation (LoRA) fine-tuning. We evaluated sequential multi-site fine-tuning, where the model is trained locally and only the updated LoRA weights are transferred to the next site. We compared this against joint fine-tuning, which requires pooling all multi-site patient data centrally before training. Performance was measured by micro F1-scores for 2 distinct subtasks: mobility extraction and impairment classification. Results: Sequential multi-site fine-tuning yielded comparable results to centralized joint fine-tuning for mobility extraction (F1, 0.861 vs 0.894) and impairment classification (F1, 0.912 vs 0.900). Both sequential and joint fine-tuning outperformed an untuned 70B model. Additionally, single-site LoRA models showed robust cross-site generalization. Discussion: Sequential multi-site fine-tuning offers a resource-friendly approach to adapt LLMs to clinical environments. By retaining previously acquired knowledge without severe interference, this strategy allows for local fine-tuning at each institution without the need to pool or share sensitive patient data required for joint fine-tuning. Conclusion: Sequential multi-site fine-tuning provides a viable solution for the scalable, incremental deployment of LLMs across institutions, showing promising generalizability for clinical information extraction from electronic health record narratives.

title: MaternalU5Triage AI Technical White Paper
authors: Jeremiah Ngene
source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: Description MaternalU5Triage: An AI-Powered Clinical Decision Support System for Maternal, Neonatal and Under-Five Emergency Triage is a comprehensive technical white paper describing the design, development, implementation, clinical validation, and future evolution of an artificial intelligence (AI)-enabled Clinical Decision Support System (CDSS) for maternal, neonatal, and under-five emergency care. The platform was developed to strengthen emergency triage, risk stratification, referral decision-making, and continuity of care by providing healthcare professionals with transparent, evidence-based, and explainable AI-assisted clinical recommendations. MaternalU5Triage integrates deterministic clinical rules, supervised machine learning, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), Large Language Models (LLMs), knowledge graphs, and Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI) within a human-in-the-loop decision-support framework that preserves clinician oversight and accountability. The current implementation comprises a functional Android-based software prototype with implemented clinical workflows, evidence-based decision pathways, and AI-assisted reasoning capabilities. The platform has undergone multi-site proof-of-concept clinical validation at the University of Nigeria Teaching Hospital (UNTH) Parklane, Enugu, and Community Primary Health Care Centre, Abor. The evaluation involved 50 healthcare professionals and 35 representative clinical cases/patient encounters using structured clinical validation and usability assessment methods to evaluate clinical decision-support performance, workflow integration, usability, acceptability, and implementation feasibility. Evaluation findings demonstrated technical feasibility, clinical relevance, and strong user acceptance. The platform achieved 70% agreement with clinician decisions, 79% correct triage classification, an average triage completion time of 90 seconds per patient, a System Usability Scale (SUS) score of 84.2/100, 85% overall user satisfaction, and 74% intention among participants to continue using the platform. Feedback obtained during the evaluation informed iterative improvements to system functionality, user interface design, clinical workflows, and AI-assisted decision-support capabilities. This white paper documents the complete technical architecture of MaternalU5Triage, including system architecture, software architecture, AI architecture, hybrid clinical reasoning, training data strategy, Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), Explainable Artificial Intelligence (XAI), interoperability, cybersecurity, privacy and data governance, responsible AI governance, validation methodology, implementation strategy, deployment considerations, monitoring, and future development roadmap. The platform is designed to support interoperability with established healthcare information standards, including FHIR, SNOMED CT, ICD-11, and LOINC. The document is intended for researchers, clinicians, software engineers, digital health practitioners, health informaticians, policymakers, funding organizations, and implementation partners interested in trustworthy AI-enabled clinical decision support systems for maternal, newborn, and child health. It serves as both a technical reference and an implementation resource for advancing safe, explainable, and evidence-based AI applications in healthcare, particularly within low-resource and resource-constrained settings.

title: Artifact-Driven Methodology for LLM Coding Agents
authors: Herman Phil Marneweck
source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: LLM coding agents produce plausible work that too often misses the working bar, and the costly failures are quiet: a capable agent optimizes the legible completion signal and trades away what is not pinned. This paper describes an artifact-driven methodology for containing that, reached by running agents on real work over fourteen months. Its central cut is enforcement substrate. Instructions (text the agent reads) produce intent; programs (execution graphs an orchestrator runs with per-node verification) produce enforcement. Around that cut sit a spec-and-plan artifact stack; a tooling layer that grounds the agent's view of the code in structural analysis rather than narrative; a verification stack of orchestrator-enforced gates, where a mechanical check decides only what it can actually decide (artifact structure, an external side effect such as a process starting) and coding work is gated by pre-registered contracts interpreted by decorrelated, active reviewers (there is no mechanical check for whether code is right; that going-in bet failed and its failure is reported); and a principal-plus-three-window actor model (human, operator, worker, and a non-agent orchestrator) with a mechanically enforced submission gate between alignment and execution. The methodology is realized in an open-source, self-hosting reference implementation and demonstrated as Design Science Research in three regimes: greenfield, rewrite against a legacy oracle, and self-hosting. A multi-vendor trace-turn corpus provides preliminary empirical signals. The claim is deliberately bounded. No layer grounds the work; the methodology's job is to make the quiet sacrifices loud and hand the rest to the human. The bet is workflow-economic (practically usable code at less human attention), not a proof of grounded verification. Version history. v2.1: measurement-paragraph refinements (failure classes decomposed in full: 9 test / 10 code or missing deliverable / 1 unverifiable workspace, plus 3 reviewer degrades failed closed; a right-censoring bound on the recent-era zero-hollow-test finding; scope clarifications in the claim map and section 25). v2: adversarial-review fixes; measured convergence results in section 27; economics accounting in section 22; DOI on the title page. v1: initial preprint. v2.2: a controlled two-arm comparison (same model, solo vs. the full stack, decorrelated predicate-bound grading) added to the case studies; the relocation of defect detection upstream of merge stated as the load-bearing empirical claim, evidenced at two independent grains; marginal-cost accounting for the verification layer.

title: From Assistants to Agents: Exploring Efficiency and Human Agency in AI-Supported Programming
authors: Carmen Laura Janina Appelt; Adrian Glauben
source_name: Journal of the Association for Information Systems
abstract: LLM-based agents are reshaping software engineering, yet empirical evidence on their practical effects remains limited. This study provides a controlled comparison between an IDE-integrated assistant, GitHub Copilot Ask, and an LLM-based agent, GitHub Copilot Agent, during brownfield onboarding tasks. In an experiment with 24 developers, we measured productivity, perceived workload, interaction patterns, and prompt behaviour using the SPACE framework. Copilot Agent reduced mean task completion time by 61.7% and NASA-TLX workload by 57.4%, while code correctness did not significantly improve. However, interaction data show a shift from active collaboration to passive supervision, raising concerns about over-reliance and skill erosion.

title: Artifact-Driven Methodology for LLM Coding Agents
authors: Herman Phil Marneweck
source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: LLM coding agents produce plausible work that too often misses the working bar, and the costly failures are quiet: a capable agent optimizes the legible completion signal and trades away what is not pinned. This paper describes an artifact-driven methodology for containing that, reached by running agents on real work over fourteen months. Its central cut is enforcement substrate. Instructions (text the agent reads) produce intent; programs (execution graphs an orchestrator runs with per-node verification) produce enforcement. Around that cut sit a spec-and-plan artifact stack; a tooling layer that grounds the agent's view of the code in structural analysis rather than narrative; a verification stack of orchestrator-enforced gates, where a mechanical check decides only what it can actually decide (artifact structure, an external side effect such as a process starting) and coding work is gated by pre-registered contracts interpreted by decorrelated, active reviewers (there is no mechanical check for whether code is right; that going-in bet failed and its failure is reported); and a principal-plus-three-window actor model (human, operator, worker, and a non-agent orchestrator) with a mechanically enforced submission gate between alignment and execution. The methodology is realized in an open-source, self-hosting reference implementation and demonstrated as Design Science Research in three regimes: greenfield, rewrite against a legacy oracle, and self-hosting. A multi-vendor trace-turn corpus provides preliminary empirical signals. The claim is deliberately bounded. No layer grounds the work; the methodology's job is to make the quiet sacrifices loud and hand the rest to the human. The bet is workflow-economic (practically usable code at less human attention), not a proof of grounded verification.

title: LLM-Guided Transportation Hub Capacity Planning with Textual Business Inputs
authors: Xiaoyue Liu; Zheng Dong
abstract: While traditional hub capacity planning models optimize effectively for quantitative inputs, they often fail to digest qualitative business context. We propose a novel framework where a large language model (LLM) agent iteratively proposes hub capacity decisions guided by natural-language business context descriptions. The key mechanism is a chain-of-thought reasoning protocol: the LLM constructs a structured decision table that maps each contextual item to specific capacity adjustments based on the implied direction and magnitude of changes. The new capacity decision is then validated through a feedback loop with an optimization model, which provides routing-based performance metrics to guide the agent's selection. On a real-world 13-hub freight network in the southeastern US, our framework achieves a 2.8% optimality gap relative to the hidden ground-truth, a significant improvement over the 11.0% gap produced by the traditional optimization model without textual business inputs. This demonstrates that LLMs can serve as a contextual bridge, integrating qualitative business insights into Operations Research workflows.

title: Uso de la inteligencia artificial para reducir los tiempos de producción en la gestión de eventos recreativos corporativos
authors: Giancarlo Castillo Ghiotto
abstract: Introduction. Corporate recreational event agencies often rely on manual routines that extend production cycles and increase rework. This study examines whether adopting generative AI is associated with reduced event production time. Methodology. A quasi-experimental before–after single-case design was conducted in a corporate recreational events company (Bogotá, Colombia) between June and September 2025. Three comparable events were produced under a traditional approach (no AI) and then with systematic ChatGPT support for creative and administrative tasks (concept development, proposal drafting, budgeting, and supplier selection). The dependent variable was total production time (hours) from brief reception to final approval. Given the small sample, the analysis prioritized paired differences, confidence intervals, and effect sizes. Results. A consistent reduction in total production time was observed across events (51 h, 60 h, and 69 h), yielding an average saving of 60 h (19.1%). The largest savings occurred in Concept Development (23.3 h) and Proposal Preparation (20.0 h), while Final Validation slightly increased (+1.3 h), reflecting additional quality checks. Conclusions. Findings suggest generative AI can be an efficiency lever for mid-sized agencies when combined with governance, training, and human verification. Results should be interpreted as applied and exploratory due to the small sample and single organizational setting. Future research should test replicability with more events and additional outcomes (cost, quality, and client satisfaction).

title: Whole body CT attenuation and volume charts from routine clinical scans via LLM report filtering
authors: Christian Wachinger; Bernhard C. Renger; Christopher Späth; Jan Stefan Kirschke; Marcus Makowski
abstract: Interpreting quantitative CT biomarkers, such as organ volume and tissue attenuation, requires large-scale healthy reference distributions. However, creating these is challenging because clinical datasets are often heavily enriched with pathology. Here, we develop an evidence-grounded, cross-verified large language model (LLM) ensemble to filter pathological findings from radiology reports, enabling the construction of pathology-reduced cohorts from over 350,000 CT examinations. Five LLMs, first, flag structure-level abnormality candidates grounded in verbatim report evidence and, second, resolve disagreements via cross-verification. Using distribution-aware generalized additive models for location, scale, and shape, we establish comprehensive whole-body reference charts for 106 anatomical structures (volumes and attenuation) across adulthood, accounting for age, sex, contrast enhancement, and acquisition parameters. Longitudinal analyses reveal structure- and contrast-dependent changes distinct from cross-sectional trends. These resources facilitate covariate-adjusted centile scoring from routine CT, supporting standardized quantitative phenotyping, multi-site imaging studies, and scalable opportunistic screening research.

title: Coresets Before Score Sets: Evaluation-Unsupervised Prompt Subset Selection for LLM Benchmarks
authors: Jihan Yao; Gantavya Bhatt; Arnav Das; Peter Jin; Ke Bao; Qiaolin Yu; Khushi Bhardwaj; Chang Su; Jialei Wang; Yikai Zhu; Sugam Devare; Damon Mosk-Aoyama; Zhen Dong; Venkatesh Srinivasan; Yineng Zhang; Oleksii Kuchaiev; Jiantao Jiao; Banghua Zhu; Jeff Bilmes
abstract: We study LLM benchmark coreset selection: selecting a small subset of prompts over multiple benchmarks whose induced model scores and rankings approximate those obtained from the full benchmark suite. In evaluation-unsupervised benchmark coreset selection (our approach), the selection algorithm uses no model evaluation outcomes, and operates on a fine granularity by producing subsets of prompts over multiple benchmarks rather than producing a sub-collection of entire benchmarks. We use submodular subset selection, and we develop and evaluate many different submodular functions for this purpose, including determinantal point process (DPP) based approaches, submodular mutual information functions, and facility location-based functions. On a new large-scale suite of 35 heterogeneous benchmarks spanning five different capability categories, 18 frontier LLMs, and over 61K prompts, we find that the facility location (FL) function operating exclusively on inexpensive semantic prompt embeddings preserves LLM scores better than twelve separate score-based and diversity-based baselines, across a range of coreset budgets. Moreover, we show our proposed objective is not limited to the evaluation-unsupervised regime: in the setting where only a handful of whole benchmarks must be selected and a large amount of model scores are available, the same objective matches or outperforms state-of-the-art baselines on the MMLU and MTEB leaderboards, while being substantially cheaper to compute. Together, our results suggest that submodularity, in general, is a strong and reliable tool for benchmark compression.

title: Bridging ERP Complexity Through Retrieval-Augmented Generation: Design and Evaluation of an Intelligent Question-Answering System for SMEs
authors: Pongsathon Pookduang; Wirapong Chansanam
abstract: Purpose/Background: Small and medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) that deploy Enterprise Resource Planning (ERP) systems face a persistent paradox: although ERP centralises organisational data, frontline users frequently lack the technical expertise to navigate complex menu structures, preventing efficient information retrieval for decision-making. This study presents a preliminary Research and Development (R&D) effort to design, build, and qualitatively evaluate a prototype intelligent question-answering system that connects to Odoo ERP through application programming interfaces (APIs) via Retrieval-Augmented Generation (RAG), enabling natural-language access to real SME business data. Methods: A single-organisation R&D case study was conducted at an SME in Khon Kaen Province, Thailand. The development cycle comprised problem analysis and requirement specification, system architecture design, prototype construction, integration and deployment, iterative testing and refinement, and multidimensional evaluation. The prototype was implemented with Chainlit (conversational interface), FastAPI (orchestration and tool-calling layer), and Odoo XML-RPC/JSON-RPC APIs (structured data retrieval). A fixed set of 20 test questions spanning four complexity levels (easy, moderate, complex, out-of-scope) was evaluated by three automated tools (OpenAI Evals, DeepEval, Ragas), by real-task verification against live ERP data, by five domain experts using 5-point Likert-scale questionnaires, and by three end users from the case-study organisation, who additionally completed the System Usability Scale (SUS). Given the very small expert and user samples, all human evaluation results are reported descriptively as preliminary, exploratory indicators rather than as statistically generalisable measures. Results: Automated evaluation achieved indicative pass rates of 95.00% (OpenAI Evals, 19/20), 90.00% (Ragas, 18/20), and 85.00% (DeepEval, 17/20). Descriptive expert feedback (n = 5) yielded an overall mean of 3.82 (high level), and descriptive end-user feedback (n = 3) yielded an overall satisfaction mean of 4.33 (highest level). The SUS score was 66.67/100, sitting at the boundary between ‘OK’ and ‘Good’ and revealing a divergence between high stated satisfaction and lower confidence in independent system use (item 9, raw mean = 2.33) and a stronger perceived need for expert assistance (item 4, raw mean = 2.67). These results are interpreted as preliminary diagnostic signals for further development rather than as confirmatory evidence. Conclusions: This preliminary R&D study suggests that a RAG-based ERP chatbot can meaningfully simplify ERP data access for SME users, while exposing persistent gaps in multi-step reasoning, user confidence, and data privacy boundaries that must be addressed in subsequent development cycles. The SUS pattern, in particular, suggests a ‘novelty effect’ in which users are enthusiastic about the natural-language interface yet remain anxious about correctness and stability during real tasks. Originality/Value: This work contributes a transparent, replicable preliminary R&D blueprint that combines (i) live API-mediated RAG over structured ERP data, (ii) a complementary multi-tool automated evaluation set (OpenAI Evals + DeepEval + Ragas), (iii) descriptive expert and end-user feedback, and (iv) SUS-based usability assessment, all documented for a single Thai SME using Odoo 18. The study explicitly positions itself as an early step toward larger, multi-site, and on-premise deployments of trustworthy ERP-integrated conversational agents.

title: Institutional Adaptation and Technological Shock: The Role of AI Regulation in Startup Financing
authors: Yunshu Ling; Ke Rong; Di Zhou
abstract: Prior research shows that technological breakthroughs heighten market uncertainty and complicate capital allocation for investors. Further, regulatory tech interventions often constrain innovation and venture investment. Despite growing attention to both streams, we still lack a systematic understanding of how regulation moderates technological shocks to shape investment. In this paper, we study the impact of two shocks on China's entrepreneurial finance system - the introduction of generative AI and AI regulation. title: Selecting Generative AI Systems for Education and Business in 2026: A Capability–Risk Framework for Comparing Frontier and Open-Weight Model Ecosystems
authors: Shiaondo Kenneth Chia
abstract: Background: Generative AI procurement is increasingly difficult because model capability, tool access, multimodality, deployment control, safety controls and pricing evolve faster than conventional technology-selection cycles. Objective: This article constructs a five-system comparison time-stamped, evidence-disciplined framework for selecting generative AI systems in education and business. Methods: A critical comparative review triangulated independent evaluation scholarship with official model and system documentation available through 29 August 2026. The review considers GPT-5.6 Sol, Claude Opus 5, Gemini 3.1 Pro, DeepSeek-V4-Pro and Llama 4 Maverick as representative ecosystems rather than treating vendor benchmark claims as directly commensurable scores. Results: The comparison shows persistent trade-offs. Closed frontier systems provide strong managed capabilities and integrated tools but create dependence on provider controls, pricing and service architecture. Open-weight models provide greater deployment and adaptation control but shift security, evaluation and governance burdens to the adopter. Multimodality, context length and agent functionality are increasingly common, making grounding quality, workflow control, data governance, evaluation discipline and total cost of ownership more discriminating than a single benchmark rank. Conclusion: Organizations should replace model leaderboards with use-case portfolios, risk tiers and repeatable local evaluations. The best system is the one that achieves acceptable task quality under the institution’s evidence, privacy, safety, latency, cost and audit requirements.

title: DIGITAL TWIN AND AI-DRIVEN SMART MANUFACTURING SYSTEMS
authors: Praveen S. Atigre; Indrajeet S. Patil; Rajan D. Patil; Sawant Amol S
abstract: The concept of Digital Twin technology has become an important factor in enabling intelligent manufacturing through the creation of dynamic virtual models of physical entities, manufacturing processes, and manufacturing systems. With the use of Digital Twins alongside with AI, IIoT, cloud computing, and cyber-physical systems, manufacturers can monitor their operations in real time, carry out predictive analysis, make autonomous decisions, and optimize the entire process life cycle. This chapter highlights a thorough discussion of digital twins and AI-based smart manufacturing systems from the viewpoint of sustainable mechanical engineering. It reviews the basic concepts and structure of digital twins along with the influence of artificial intelligence, machine learning, predictive maintenance, intelligent process optimization, and quality control in modern manufacturing. This chapter also reviews the applications of digital twins in the context of smart factories, additive manufacturing, robotics, energy management, and supply chain optimization to boost productivity and sustainability in manufacturing. The importance of digital twin technology for resource efficiency, reduction of carbon footprint, circular manufacturing, and net-zero manufacturing processes is also reviewed. This chapter finally discusses the existing challenges associated with data compatibility, cybersecurity, computational intensity, and industrial scalability, along with future perspectives that may include generative AI, edge intelligence, autonomous factories, and human-centric Industry 5.0.

title: Capturing Technological Windows: Configurations of Capabilities and Responses Toward Innovations
authors: Zhou Liang; Ruicong Xiao
abstract: Technological windows create both significant potential and profound uncertainty for firms, yet firms exposed to the same window often exhibit different innovation outcomes. Drawing on a configurational perspective, this study investigates how firms’ capability foundations and response patterns jointly shape technological innovation performance when a technological window opens. Using the emergence of generative artificial intelligence, marked by the release of OpenAI’s ChatGPT, as a representative technological window, we analyze Chinese listed firms by fuzzy-set Qualitative Comparative Analysis (fsQCA) to identify configurations of capability foundations (knowledge base and recombinant capabilities) and response patterns (the timing and scale of human capital investment), while accounting for environmental contingencies. The findings reveal that technological innovation under opportunity windows is not driven by opportunity exposure or resource input alone, but emerges from specific alignments between capability foundations and response patterns. Multiple equifinal pathways lead to high technological innovation, whereas misalignment consistently results in low innovation outcomes, even under the same technological window. By reconceptualizing technological innovation as a configurational and processual outcome, this study advances research on technological windows and innovation management, and offers a new framework for understanding firm heterogeneity in responding to transformative technological change.

title: QueueBreak: A Trace-to-Diagnosis Pipeline for Tail Latency in Agentic LLM Services
authors: Xingrao Ma; Zongxi Li; Chengzu Dong; Di Shao; Xiao Liu
source_name: IEEE International Conference on Web Services (ICWS)
abstract: Agentic large language model (LLM) services execute a user request as a workflow that interleaves model invocations with external tool calls. When workflow p99 grows, end-to-end latency alone cannot reveal whether the tail accumulates before execution starts or within execution; these regimes require different operational remedies. We present QueueBreak, a workflow-aware trace-to-diagnosis (T2D) framework that reconstructs request arrival, first-step start, and completion from lightweight workflow logs and step traces. QueueBreak decomposes each workflow before aggregating tail statistics, reports a Queue Dominance Signature, and checks the diagnosis through load-reduction intervention. Across load escalation, dependency degradation, and intervention, the evaluated service shows the same pattern: tail growth is dominated by pre-execution waiting while execution remains stable. In a mixed-workload sweep, total p99 rises from 21.25s to 165.40s as pre-execution p99 rises from 11.67s to 144.04s, whereas stress execution p99 is 16.80s. With tool failure (pfail=0.2), total p99 reaches 978.81s and the mean preexecution fraction reaches 0.923. Reducing load to one quarter of the stress rate cuts pre-execution p99 from 579.2s to 17.3s while execution p99 changes only from 18.0s to 17.5s. These results identify admission control and workflow-aware capacity planning as primary QoS recovery levers.

title: ROSA: A Robotics Foundation Model Serving System for Robot Factories
authors: Wenqi Jiang; Jason Clemons; Rowland O’Flaherty; Hugo Hadfield; Alperen Değirmenci; Shuran Song; Yashraj Narang; Christos Kozyrakis
abstract: Robotics foundation models (RFMs) are making general-purpose robots increasingly practical for factory deployments. While RFM serving systems are central to this vision, existing systems are largely shaped by a single-robot, single-model assumption: inference is treated as an edge-computing problem handled by an on-robot or dedicated nearby GPU, and the serving objective is to minimize the latency of a single action model. In this paper, we propose ROSA, an RFM serving system for robot factories designed around three key principles. First, ROSA adopts shared GPU-pool serving, allowing a fleet of robots to access powerful server-class GPUs over the network in order to improve inference performance, battery duration, and GPU utilization. Second, ROSA provides a robotics-aware programming abstraction and system design that supports multi-model pipelines, per-task performance requirements, and failure handling. Third, ROSA uses factory-objective-driven scheduling to maximize SLO-qualified factory productivity rather than minimizing individual request latency. We implement ROSA on top of Ray Serve for distributed orchestration, with vLLM, PyTorch, and JAX as model-serving backends, and evaluate it on both real robots and synthetic large-scale workloads. The results show that ROSA improves factory productivity by up to 12.06x over conventional dedicated serving systems.

title: Inqeduagent: Adaptive AI Learning Partners with Gaussian Process Augmentation
authors: Wen-Xi Yang; Tian-Fang Zhao; Guan Liu
source_name: Asia Conference on Machine Learning and Computing (ACMLC)
abstract: Collaborative partnerships play a crucial role in inquiry-oriented education. However, most learning partners are currently assigned through experience-driven heuristics or rule-based machine assistants, which often result in limited knowledge expansion and low adaptability. To address these challenges, this study introduces InqEduAgent, an LLM-empowered generative agent framework designed to simulate and select adaptive learning partners for inquiry-based learning. InqEduAgent integrates a Gaussian process-augmented matching mechanism to model the cognitive and evaluative characteristics of learners, allowing adaptive partner selection based on prior knowledge patterns. Comprehensive experiments demonstrate that InqEduAgent consistently achieves superior performance across diverse learning scenarios and large language model configurations. This study advances human-AI collaborative learning by enabling intelligent pairing between human- and AI-based learning partners, and contributes to adaptive user modeling and personalized recommendation within Web-based educational environments.

title: Organizing Immersion: A Sociomaterial Study of AI-Driven Non-Wearable Interactive Environments
authors: C.Y. Wang; Zhuojun Li; Y W Su
abstract: Sociomaterial research has fundamentally reshaped how scholars understand the constitutive entanglement of technology and organizing. Yet, despite its ontological commitments, existing empirical studies have largely examined technologies that remain experientially distinguishable as bounded artifacts—such as tools, systems, or platforms. This paper examines what happens when this implicit artifact-centered anchoring no longer holds. Even studies that emphasize fluidity, performativity, or becoming typically rely on empirical settings in which technologies retain identifiable material forms, interfaces, or systems that can be analytically foregrounded. Drawing on a qualitative, multi-site study of AI-driven, non-wearable immersive environments in experiential service settings, this study advances a design-oriented framework in which technology operates as a responsive environment rather than a discrete artifact. Centered on immersive narrative dining, the framework articulates an end-to-end automated pipeline that integrates multimodal generative AI, spatial computing, and real-time sensor-driven interaction, offering a replicable model for the design of next-generation experiential services. Our findings identify three shifts that challenge artifact-centered applications of sociomaterial theory: (1) organizational action emerges through environmental participation rather than artifact interaction; (2) managerial control is enacted through continuous calibration of environmental responsiveness rather than governance of stable systems; and (3) organizational routines stabilize as adaptive, improvisational patterns co-evolving with responsive environments. Theoretically, we argue that AI-driven immersive environments represent a boundary condition for artifact-centered sociomaterial theorizing and call for an extension that accounts for responsive sociotechnical environments. We contribute to Technology and Innovation Management research by showing how innovation increasingly involves designing and governing generative environments rather than implementing discrete technological artifacts, thereby reframing core assumptions about control, value creation, and organizational capability in AI-enabled contexts.

title: Intelligent Datacenter Networks: Integrating Software-Defined Networking, Artificial Intelligence, and Autonomous Network Operations
authors: Jacob Sean
source_name: International Journal of Advance Industrial Engineering
abstract: The rapid growth of cloud-native applications, large-scale artificial intelligence workloads, and latency-sensitive edge services has placed unprecedented demands on datacenter network infrastructure. In response, the networking industry is converging around three transformative paradigms: Software-Defined Networking (SDN), which decouples control logic from forwarding hardware to enable centralized programmability; Artificial Intelligence for networking (AI4Net), which applies machine learning to traffic optimization, anomaly detection, and capacity planning; and Autonomous Network Operations (ANO), which aspires to closed-loop, self-configuring, self-optimizing, and self-healing network management with minimal human intervention. This paper presents a comprehensive, integrated survey of these three paradigms and their synergistic convergence in modern datacenter environments. We begin by examining the architectural evolution of SDN from early OpenFlow-centric designs to contemporary intent-driven, multi-layer control platforms that govern network, compute, and storage resources holistically. We then survey AI-driven networking techniques, including deep reinforcement learning for traffic engineering, graph neural networks for topology-aware optimization, transformer-based models for network telemetry analysis, and generative AI for configuration synthesis. Next, we analyze autonomous network operations frameworks, covering closed-loop automation architectures, digital twin-based validation, formal verification of network invariants, and trust and explainability requirements for human-machine teaming. We further investigate cross-cutting concerns including programmable data planes, network security automation, multi-domain orchestration, and energy-efficient networking. Finally, we identify open research challenges and chart future directions toward fully intelligent, self-driving datacenter networks. By synthesizing insights from over 80 references spanning academic research, industry practice, and standards development, this article provides a unified reference for researchers, architects, and practitioners working at the intersection of networking, AI, and autonomous systems.

title: Editorial: Digital transformation in transport and logistics
authors: Ralf M. Elbert; Hongjun Wu
abstract: The digital transformation of transport and logistics has moved from a strategic aspiration to an operational necessity. The intellectual origins of this shift trace back to the Industry 4.0 initiative of the early 2010s, when the integration of cyber-physical systems placed digital-physical convergence at the center of industrial strategy (Kagermann, 2013; Sullivan and Kern, 2021). For much of that decade, however, the practical distance between vision and reality remained wide.What narrowed this gap was the rapid development of enabling technologies. Internet of Things (IoT) devices, cloud computing, machine learning and autonomous systems such as Automated Guided Vehicles (AGVs) and warehouse robots moved from experimental settings into live logistics operations (Fottner et al., 2021; Fragapane et al., 2021; Escherle et al., 2023; Lam et al., 2024). A growing body of research has documented the resulting improvements in visibility, asset utilization and decision-making capability across the value chain. Industry 4.0 has positioned digital technologies as central enablers of this transformation (Barreto et al., 2017). IoT devices now provide real-time visibility into the movement and condition of goods across extended transport chains (Barreto et al., 2017; Feng and Ye, 2021). Artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning algorithms support demand forecasting, route optimization and predictive maintenance (Hoffmann et al., 2022; Nitsche et al., 2024). Cloud computing and digital platforms facilitate the integration of fragmented logistics ecosystems by connecting shippers, carriers, terminal operators and end customers through shared data environments (Winkelhaus and Grosse, 2020).The 2020s then introduced a different kind of pressure. The COVID-19 pandemic and subsequent geopolitical disruptions revealed the fragility of efficiency-optimized but resilience-deficient logistics networks. Contact restrictions, acute labor shortages and simultaneous demand shocks forced many organizations to compress years of planned digitalization into months (Ivanov, 2021; Hellweg et al., 2023). The resulting recalibration was structural. End-to-end supply chain visibility and data-driven decision-making became operational necessities rather than competitive advantages, and the need to collect, integrate and act on operational data intensified across the industry.The consequence is a rapidly growing number of interfaces among physical assets, digital tools and humans throughout the transport and logistics value chain. Figure 1 illustrates them as a three-level architecture: at the physical level, physical assets (e.g. vehicles and facilities), field and IoT devices generate ongoing data about what is happening in the logistics system; at the digital level, these data are ingested, stored, integrated and exchanged across systems through application programming interfaces (APIs) and related system connections, where they support event management, interoperability and consistent digital representations of operations; these representations provide the basis for data-driven analytics and decision-making at the analytical level, such as diagnostic assessments of current system states, predictive analytics for future developments, reality-based scenario analysis and higher-level decision support. The analytical outputs, in turn, move downward to shape physical behavior through accurate and reliable control signals (Albrecht et al., 2024). This bidirectional architecture has considerable productive potential. However, realizing it requires ensuring that digital systems can accurately capture the complexity of the physical world and that analytical outputs can be effectively translated into operational decisions.This special issue of Logistics Research was designed to address these dual challenges. It invited analytical, conceptual, empirical, experimental and optimization contributions that advance the understanding of digital and technological interfaces in transport and logistics at both the technological and the organizational-planning levels. In particular, the integration of digital technologies into physical assets and processes, as well as the application of data-driven analytical methods for supply chain decision-making, were identified as areas of primary interest. The two contributions of this special issue, Wehner (2026) and Doege (2026), address two essential and complementary dimensions of this transformation though different in scope and methodology: the physical implementation of autonomous technologies and the analytical use of network data for resilience.Digital interfaces in transport and logistics differ fundamentally in the nature of the problems they address and the level at which those problems arise. To position this heterogeneity, we propose a two-dimensional conceptual framework that distinguishes between the nature of the digital interface, depending on whether digital technologies primarily sense, translate and control physical assets (physical-digital interface) or act on digital representations of them (analytical-digital interface). This framework also distinguishes between the levels of analysis at which challenges and decisions arise for specific operations and technologies or across network-level coordination. These two dimensions are analytically necessary because operational and network-level challenges differ in scope, time horizon and coordination requirements, while the two interface types raise distinct technological and organizational issues. Table 1 maps this space through selected examples. The two contributions in this special issue occupy distinct positions within this space, as discussed in Section 2.3.This framework reflects observations drawn from a broader community, including discussions within the production, logistics and transportation research community, including exchanges at the 7th Interdisciplinary Conference on Production, Logistics and Traffic (ICPLT), held in Darmstadt in March 2025. These discussions covered the full spectrum from physical automation to network-level analytics across rail freight, road transport, maritime logistics, urban delivery and terminal operations.Physical-digital interfaces refer to the points at which physical assets (e.g. robots, vehicles, containers and terminal equipment) become readable by digital systems and at which digital instructions are translated into physical behavior. Lee et al. (2015) proposed a five-layer architecture for cyber-physical systems that precisely captures this bidirectional flow from physical sensing to digital action, spanning connection, conversion, cyber, cognition and configuration. At both the operational and the network levels, the challenges are primarily technological. For example, how can an autonomous system reliably perceive and act in a dynamic, unstructured environment, and how can the resulting information be safely shared and made interoperable across various systems (Kembro et al., 2017; Fottner et al., 2021)? Beyond the technical dimension, physical-digital interfaces raise equally significant organizational questions. The introduction of autonomous systems into existing workflows requires process re-engineering, personnel retraining and often fundamental rethinking of task allocation between humans and machines (Cichosz et al., 2020; Hellweg et al., 2023).Analytical-digital interfaces are the boundaries between digital representations of the real world and the computational methods used to extract useful information from them. The central challenge here is epistemological: What data and metrics are sufficient for effective decision-making, and how much network visibility is actually needed? The growing availability of various data sources has considerably expanded the scope of these interfaces. Yet data availability alone does not guarantee usefulness. Supply chain networks are characterized by information asymmetries, data quality issues and coordination failures, and autonomous entities typically make decisions based on local and incomplete information, so that what any single actor can reliably infer and influence remains limited (Delfmann et al., 2018; Fottner et al., 2021). Therefore, the practical value of digital analysis at this interface depends on whether data-driven decision rules and performance indicators can be translated into operationally feasible actions in specific organizational and network contexts.The two contributions in this special issue occupy complementary positions within the framework proposed above. Together, they illustrate how digital transformation in transport and logistics unfolds through two distinct but interconnected modes: the physical implementation of autonomous technologies and the analytical use of network-level data for resilience-oriented decision-making.Wehner (2026) are positioned at the physical-digital interface on the operational level. Their empirical study investigates the integration of automation and digital technologies in air cargo logistics through the empirical testing of the O3dyn pallet transport robot at Munich Airport. This study documents a ten-day real-world trial in which the robot's performance was assessed across multiple transport scenarios, with data collected on travel times, load weights, manual interventions and operational challenges.Doege (2026) are positioned at the analytical-digital interface on the network level, addressing one concrete analytical question: How can supply chain networks be made more resilient against disruption propagation, and how much network visibility is actually required for this purpose? Using agent-based modeling combined with a susceptible-infected-recovered epidemiological framework, the authors simulate disruption cascades across ten real-world supply chain networks and evaluate five node-selection strategies derived from social network analysis metrics.Digital transformation in transport and logistics has moved past the stage of technology demonstration into a period that requires empirically grounded and organizationally sensitive research. The two-dimensional framework proposed here offers a means of positioning and connecting contributions across this field. The papers in this special issue represent two reference points in that space. Viewed through this framework, their respective scopes point directly toward the most consequential open research directions. Yet the scope of the present issue necessarily remains selective. Some important dimensions are not addressed directly.The interfaces among the physical, digital and analytical levels are not independent. Digital twins represent the most developed form of this interdependence, functioning simultaneously as physical-digital synchronization mechanisms and as analytical simulation environments (Tao et al., 2018; Fottner et al., 2021). While a growing body of research has begun to explore their potential in logistics and supply chain management, this dimension falls outside the scope of the present issue and warrants continued attention, particularly in multi-actor and cross-modal settings where the integration of operational data streams with network-level decision support remains technically and organizationally demanding.Furthermore, the rapid emergence of generative AI and large language models represents the most visible frontier. Applications such as natural language interfaces for freight procurement, generative scenario planning for supply chain risk and AI-assisted coordination across carrier networks demonstrate the remarkable potential of these disruptive technologies in logistics decision-making. While these applications are situated at the analytical-digital interface, they also introduce new challenges regarding model interpretability and human oversight. As the submission timelines preceded this period, these developments are not addressed in this special issue. However, they do deserve more focused attention in future research.The contributions in this special issue encourage further inquiry at the intersection of physical automation and network intelligence, advancing both the technological and the organizational foundations of digital transformation in transport and logistics.During the preparation of this work, the authors used Grammarly and Claude in the writing process to improve the readability and language of the manuscript. After using this tool/service, the authors reviewed and edited the content as needed and take full responsibility for the content of the published article.The Guest Editors wish to thank all authors who responded to the call for papers, the anonymous reviewers whose expertise ensured the quality of the review process and the Editor-in-Chief of Logistics Research for the opportunity to organize this special issue. They also wish to acknowledge the organizers and participants of the 7th Interdisciplinary Conference on Production, Logistics and Traffic, whose presentations and discussions on digital transformation in transport and logistics provided a broader intellectual context for this special issue.

title: ACCOUNTING AND ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE
authors: Ahmad Omar Hardan
abstract: Accounting and Artificial Intelligence: Transforming Financial Reporting, Auditing, and Decision-Making in the Digital Age presents a comprehensive exploration of how artificial intelligence is fundamentally reshaping the accounting profession. Authored by Ahmad Omar Hardan, this book positions AI not merely as a technological tool but as a transformative force that redefines the very essence of accounting practice—from transaction processing and financial reporting to auditing, taxation, and strategic decision-making. Through its systematic integration of AI technologies—including machine learning, natural language processing, robotic process automation, and generative AI—with core accounting functions, this volume demonstrates how financial professionals can harness intelligent systems to enhance accuracy, efficiency, and insight. The book traces the evolution of accounting from manual bookkeeping through the digital revolution to the current AI-driven paradigm, emphasizing the potential of these technologies to address perennial challenges such as fraud detection, regulatory compliance, and real-time financial analysis. It examines the strategic frameworks, operational structures, and ethical governance systems that underpin successful AI adoption in accounting, offering a benchmark for firms and institutions worldwide. With a forward-looking lens, the author articulates a vision of accounting where intelligent automation complements human expertise—where technology becomes a catalyst for deeper analytical insight, strategic advisory, and sustainable value creation. In the era of digital transformation, artificial intelligence has evolved from a futuristic concept into a defining force reshaping the global accounting landscape. Accounting and Artificial Intelligence: Transforming Financial Reporting, Auditing, and Decision-Making in the Digital Age by Ahmad Omar Hardan presents an in-depth study of how AI technologies are revolutionizing accounting practice. The book delves into how strategic alignment of AI with core accounting functions—from bookkeeping and financial reporting to auditing, taxation, and management accounting—enhances accuracy, efficiency, and strategic value creation for both organizations and stakeholders. At its core, this work situates AI within a broader transformation of the accounting profession—one that reconciles technological capability with professional judgment and ethical responsibility. Through empirical analysis and conceptual exploration, it demonstrates how AI-powered systems translate vast amounts of financial data into actionable insights, predictive analytics, and real-time decision support. The study highlights key operational frameworks, from automated transaction processing and continuous auditing to AI-driven risk assessment and fraud detection systems. Ahmad Omar Hardan elucidates how regulatory environments, institutional innovation, and socioeconomic contexts converge to support the adoption of AI in accounting. The narrative underscores that AI is not merely a technological upgrade but a fundamental reimagining of how financial information is captured, processed, analyzed, and communicated. It also addresses the multi-dimensional challenges—regulatory, ethical, technical, and organizational—that must be navigated to ensure that AI adoption yields tangible and responsible outcomes. By situating AI adoption within global comparative frameworks, the book articulates the emergence of AI-augmented accounting as a new paradigm in financial management. It argues that an integrated approach—balancing innovation, transparency, and professional skepticism—offers a replicable model for accounting firms, corporations, and regulators worldwide. Ultimately, this work envisions a future where accounting becomes a strategic partner in organizational success, underscoring that the prosperity of businesses and economies depends not on traditional record-keeping alone but on the capacity to leverage intelligent technologies for deeper insight and forward-looking decision-making. The landscape of accounting is evolving rapidly, with artificial intelligence at its core. Accounting and Artificial Intelligence: Transforming Financial Reporting, Auditing, and Decision-Making in the Digital Age delves into how AI technologies are pioneering transformative approaches that align financial accuracy with efficiency, insight, and strategic value. This book explores the mechanisms by which accounting functions integrate AI to ensure long-term organizational resilience, regulatory compliance, and stakeholder trust. Authored by Ahmad Omar Hardan, this publication sheds light on how the accounting profession is leveraging AI to build a future where technology and professional expertise coexist synergistically. Published in 2026, this comprehensive study examines the strategic frameworks, operational variables, and policy implications that position AI-augmented accounting at the forefront of financial management. Background The accounting profession is undergoing a paradigm shift as artificial intelligence becomes a central pillar of financial operations. This book explores why accounting firms and financial departments have embraced AI-driven approaches that integrate automation, predictive analytics, and intelligent decision support. As organizations face pressing challenges—from regulatory complexity to data proliferation and fraud risks—AI stands as a model of how financial functions can drive both efficiency and strategic insight. Definition and Core Concepts AI in accounting extends beyond automation, incorporating intelligent analysis, pattern recognition, and predictive capabilities. This book elaborates on the concept by examining AI methodologies in automating transaction processing, implementing continuous auditing, and fostering strategic decision-making through advanced analytics. Underlying Phenomena The increasing demand for AI in accounting stems from data volume growth, regulatory pressures, and the need for real-time financial intelligence. The book investigates how global trends have influenced AI adoption in accounting and how regulatory frameworks support the integration of intelligent systems into financial reporting and assurance. Working Principles The operational structure of AI-augmented accounting revolves around ethical frameworks, algorithmic transparency, and continuous monitoring. title: Large Language Models as non-Player Characters in Massively Multiplayer Online Role-Playing Games: A Systematic Scoping Review
authors: Mulima Chibuye
abstract: This project is a systematic scoping review (built on a systematic, multi-database search) examining the use of large language models (LLMs) and generative AI to power non-player characters (NPCs) in video games, with a specific focus on the demands of massively multiplayer online role-playing games (MMORPGs). Traditional NPCs rely on static, scripted dialogue, which players consistently identify as an immersion barrier; LLMs offer context-aware, memory-aware, and socially flexible interaction, but their deployment at the scale, persistence, and adversarial exposure of an MMORPG raises unresolved questions of capability, player impact, engineering feasibility, and safety. The purpose of this review is to map and critically appraise the existing evidence base so that researchers and developers can understand what is currently demonstrated, what remains unproven, and what is required before responsible large-scale deployment. The review addresses four pre-specified questions, organised around a PECO framework (Population: MMORPG players and NPC systems; Exposure: LLM-driven or generative-AI NPCs; Comparator: scripted or rule-based NPC baselines; Outcomes below). (1) Capability: what can LLM-driven NPCs reliably do beyond scripted dialogue, including memory, social reasoning, action selection, and multi-agent interaction? (2) Player outcomes: do LLM-driven NPCs measurably improve immersion, engagement, believability, or usability, and under what conditions? (3) Systems constraints: which architecture patterns best bind LLM outputs to authoritative game rules, latency budgets, and content-safety constraints? (4) Risk and governance: what is required to mitigate hallucination-driven false affordances, prompt-injection exploits, and bias or toxicity harms at MMO scale? Eligible sources are peer-reviewed studies, preprints, theses, and grey-literature/industry reports (January 2020 – February 2026) reporting on generative AI or LLMs applied to game NPCs or autonomous game agents, with a retrievable methodology and available in English. Eight databases and repositories were searched (ACM Digital Library, IEEE Xplore, arXiv, PubMed, Google Scholar, GDC Vault, ProQuest Dissertations & Theses, and targeted industry repositories including NVIDIA and Inworld AI), supplemented by citation chaining of two anchor reviews. Records are screened in two stages against the eligibility criteria, data are extracted using a pre-specified structured form, risk of bias is assessed with the Mixed Methods Appraisal Tool (MMAT 2018), and certainty of evidence is appraised with a modified GRADE approach. The primary synthesis is a structured qualitative narrative organised by the four questions; quantitative synthesis is limited to studies reporting extractable comparative statistics, with the standardised mean difference (Hedges' g) as the pre-specified effect measure. Expected outcomes: the review is anticipated to show that LLM-driven NPCs are technically feasible and show directional promise for player engagement, but that the evidence base is sparse, heterogeneous, and dominated by small prototype studies and industry reports, yielding low overall certainty. We expect player-facing quantitative evidence to be extremely limited (likely a single study with combinable statistics, giving a small-to-moderate but non-significant effect with wide confidence intervals), latency and conversational failure modes to emerge as the dominant deployment barriers, and hybrid constraint-layer architectures, governed memory systems, and adversarial security testing (against prompt injection and bias/toxicity) to be identified as critical engineering and governance requirements. The intended contribution is the first PRISMA-aligned synthesis of LLM-NPC evidence framed for MMORPG deployment, alongside a research agenda calling for pre-registered, adequately powered, multi-site player evaluations. This registration is retrospective: the literature search and data extraction were conducted prior to registration. It is being deposited to provide a transparent, time-stamped record of the review's objectives, eligibility criteria, search strategy, extraction fields, and synthesis methods.

title: A Decision Support System for Rapid Deployment of Emergency Healthcare Facilities for Infectious Disease Using Augmented Large Language Models
authors: Guanying Huang; Shenghua Zhou; S Thomas Ng; Hongzhe Yue; Dezhi Li
abstract: The emergency healthcare facilities for infectious disease deployment (EHFIDD) is a crucial measure to alleviate the pressure placed on healthcare systems by public health emergencies caused by infectious outbreaks. However, the rapid EHFIDD involves short timelines, stringent quality requirements, and numerous decision points. Therefore, it is urgent to develop a decision support system (DSS) capable of guiding a scientific and efficient deployment process from site selection to final delivery within a limited timeframe. Previous studies have primarily developed rule-based and pretrained DSS for the rapid EHFIDD, which heavily relied on predefined knowledge and manual configuration, resulting in limited efficiency and scalability. To address this limitation, this study used an augmented large language model (LLM) to develop and deploy a DSS prototype for rapid EHFIDD, simultaneously achieving high development efficiency and reliable decision-making performance. Specifically, this study established an LLM-enabled knowledge graph (KG) development method tailored for EHFIDD-related standards; developed a retrieval-augmented generation (RAG)-based approach to augment six recent LLMs using EHFIDD-KG; and proposed a comprehensive evaluation system for DSS performance, including accuracy, traceability, and relevance. Results show that (1) medium-scale LLMs achieve more augmentation from EHFIDD-KG than ultralarge LLMs; (2) the augmentation is more pronounced in answering open-ended questions than closed-ended ones; (3) the augmented LLMs achieve average improvements of 0.20, 0.40, and 0.21 in accuracy, traceability, and relevance over the original model; and (4) KG containing image information outperforms text-only KG with average gains of 0.08, 0.05, and 0.12 in accuracy, traceability, and relevance. Finally, the DSS’ robustness and generalizability are discussed, alongside its theoretical contributions, managerial implications, and human-centric governance for deployment safety. This study provides a systematic and reliable methodology for DSS development in rapid EHFIDD contexts and offers a novel technical pathway for enabling explainable LLM applications in emergency engineering domains.

title: Covering the Unseen: Information Demand Coverage Optimization for Retrieval-Augmented Generation
authors: Bingxue Zhang; Jianying Jia; Feida Zhu
abstract: Retrieval-augmented generation (RAG) typically treats context selection as ranking chunks against a single query embedding. This assumption breaks down for complex queries, such as multi-hop or ambiguous questions, where top-k selection tends to over-cover one semantic aspect while ignoring critical sub-questions. We propose GeoRAG, which recasts context selection as Information Demand Coverage Optimization. GeoRAG builds a multi-dimensional demand distribution through diverse sub-query generation and reverse-validation weighting, then selects context by minimizing the Sinkhorn-Wasserstein distance between this demand distribution and the coverage of the selected set. The resulting demand-weighted facility-location objective is monotone submodular, giving a $1-1/e$ greedy guarantee, which we approximate with a Sinkhorn-based marginal-gain surrogate. The method is unsupervised, training-free, and retrieval-agnostic. We further show that single-point, query-proximity scorers cannot cover multi-modal demands, exposing a structural limit of ranking-based selection. On six open-domain QA benchmarks, GeoRAG improves exact match (EM) by +6.5 to +7.5 points over top-k truncation (up to +9.7 on HotpotQA and ASQA) and outperforms strong baselines including MMR, DPP, BGE-Reranker, SMART-RAG, and AdaGReS, with stable gains across context budgets and sub-query generators.

title: KernelSight-LM: A Kernel-Level LLM Inference Simulator
authors: Xiteng Yao; Taeho Kim; Hengzhi Pei; Xinle Liu; Kyle Ulrich; Leonard Lausen; Ashish Khetan; Xiang Song; George Karypis; Martin Herbordt
abstract: As large language models (LLMs) move into production serving, practitioners must rapidly evaluate inference performance across diverse hardware, models, and serving parameters to meet cost and latency targets. However, the end-to-end behavior of LLMs couples serving-layer policies with low-level GPU kernel execution and rapidly evolving architectures, forcing slow, deployment-specific benchmarking that is hard to generalize. We present KernelSight-LM, a fine-grained inference simulator that models token-level execution and produces kernel-level latency breakdowns. It decomposes each serving step into a roofline kernel model with a learned efficiency term, a communication model, and a host-overhead model, composed through a discrete-event scheduler that also captures mechanisms like prefix caching and continuous batching. KernelSight-LM offers two prediction tiers that trade target-GPU data for accuracy. The cross-generation tier uses no target-GPU measurements, only hardware specifications and kernel microbenchmarks from previously profiled GPUs, and predicts per-kernel latency on an unseen GPU generation to 12.1% error, a 1.8x improvement over the roofline baseline (22.0%). A second target-measured tier adds one model-agnostic kernel-microbenchmark sweep on the target GPU, sharpening per-kernel error to 3.8%, a 7.3x improvement over a comparable baseline (27.7%). Both tiers require far less target-GPU data than the prior systems they extend. In our simulator, these predictions yield end-to-end median (p50) errors across six model families of 15.4%, 12.8%, and 3.0% (TTFT, TPOT, throughput) in the cross-generation tier and 14.3%, 6.2%, and 2.7% in the target-measured tier, matching dedicated profiling tools while collecting far less on-device data. Beyond prediction, its kernel-level bottleneck breakdowns support hardware/software co-design and capacity planning.

title: The Spatial Footprint of Artificial Intelligence: Evaluating the Friction Between Fast-Tracked Digital Infrastructure and Local Land-Use Governance in Italy
authors: Mehrdad Afshar Majd
source_name: Zenodo (CERN European Organization for Nuclear Research)
abstract: The generative AI boom has turned data centres from invisible utilities into one of the most land-, power- and water-intensive building types of the early twenty-first century. Planning theory, however, still tends to treat them through the dematerialising language of “the cloud.” This paper examines the institutional friction that the AI build-out has produced in Italy, where the national state and sub-national governments moved in opposite directions within a single quarter of 2026. Law Decree 21/2026 (Article 8) created a fast-tracked single national authorisation procedure (procedimento unico nazionale) with a binding statutory deadline of ten months, extendable to thirteen. Its purpose was to capture mobile hyperscale capital before it relocated to other European markets. Within weeks, the Lombardy region reasserted territorial control through Regional Law 11/2026, which routes large projects into supra-municipal planning agreements, requires wasteheat recovery audits, and imposes equalisation and compensation levies on built surface. We read these instruments against the actual reorganisation of Italy’s data-centre geography: the saturated Milan inference cluster, the brownfield conversion of the former Galileo Ferraris thermoelectric plant at Trino in Piedmont, and the subsea-cable and renewables story now unfolding as a “Data Center Valley” in Puglia. AI infrastructure, we argue, exposes a territorial blind spot in planning practice. We develop that argument through two distinctions: between the spatial logics of AI training and AI inference, and between data centres as engines of industrial requalification and as instruments of territorial extraction. The governance question is not whether to authorise these facilities. It is how to convert a highly automated, low-employment, resource-hungry industry, one that runs on accelerated corporate timelines, into durable local public value. That conversion requires a shift from reactive zoning toward proactive territorial equalisation.
